The architecture is built so that when such a machine exists, its output enters the plant only as an offline, gated calibration anchor that provably preserves the safety envelope — never as something in the loop. Forward-compatible with quantum hardware, without ever betting the plant on it.

What a microsecond answer buys: exploring between measurements

The 7475× calibration is not merely a headline about accuracy. It changes what the controller is allowed to do in the gaps between measurements — and to see why, you have to notice that a fusion plant does not actually watch itself continuously. It blinks.

A diagnostic does not report in an unbroken stream. It samples. A magnetic probe, a strain gauge, an interferometer — each hands the controller a fresh reading at intervals, and between two readings the plant is, in a real sense, flying on faith. It has its last measurement and it has its model, and nothing new arrives until the next sample lands. A controller that can only react to measurements is therefore idle in those gaps, waiting for the world to tell it something. That idleness is wasted time, and in a machine where a magnet can begin to fail in a microsecond, wasted time is the enemy.

Now give that controller a magnet twin that returns a full strain field — the load in every one of a coil's 82 turns — in microseconds. Suddenly the gap between two measurements is not dead time. It is rehearsal time. In the interval before the next reading lands, the controller can query the twin thousands of times, asking a stream of what-ifs: if I ramp this coil now, where does the strain peak, and does any turn approach the 0.40 percent ceiling? If I trim the field here to hold the plasma shape, what does that do to the load on the inner turns? It auditions candidate actions against the twin, discards the ones that crowd a limit, and commits only the one that keeps the most margin — all before the plant has blinked its eyes open again. Control stops waiting on the world and starts running ahead of it. That is what real-time exploration between measurements means, concretely: the machine reasons about its own near future in the pauses when it cannot see.

But exploration is only worth doing if the model you explore with can be trusted. A surrogate that is three orders of magnitude off the exact physics would send the controller chasing ghosts — rehearsing against a machine that does not exist, and committing actions tuned to a fantasy. This is exactly what the calibration buys. Dragging the magnet twin's error down by a factor of 7475, using a handful of exact high-fidelity anchors, is what makes the fast answer accurate enough to act on rather than merely glance at. The per-turn pre-load that flattens the strain across all 82 turns to 0.017 percent — comfortably inside the 0.40 percent limit — is a decision the twin is only entitled to make because its strain field is faithful to the real coil to a part in thousands. Accuracy and speed are usually a trade; calibration is the mechanism that briefly lets you refuse the trade and have both.

And the capability generalizes past the coil. The same fast, faithful surrogate that lets the controller rehearse thousands of actions between two heartbeats is the surrogate that, pointed at a design instead of a live plant, lets an engineer audition ten thousand possible machines in the time an exact solver would spend on one. Running the plant and designing the plant turn out to be the same act performed at two different speeds — which is the subject of the next section.

Cracking the optimization code

There is a second life for these fast surrogates, one that has nothing to do with running a plant, and it is the one that gives this chapter its name. A surrogate that returns a physics answer in microseconds does not merely let you control a machine. It lets you optimize one — to sculpt the machine itself, in silico, before a single bolt of it is cut from steel. This is where artificial intelligence stops being a safety net and becomes an act of imagination: it lets us audition ten thousand possible reactors and keep only the best.

Think about what designing a fusion generator actually is, underneath the physics. Stripped bare, it is a search. You have a few dozen knobs — major radius, aspect ratio, elongation, triangularity, field strength, the current, the fuel mix, the shape of the pressure profile — and each setting of those knobs is a candidate machine with its own gain, its own stress, its own neutron budget, its own price. The space of candidate machines is astronomically large, and until recently you could afford to evaluate only a handful of points in it, because each point cost hours of a slow, exact physics solver. So designers did what you do when evaluation is expensive: they picked a plausible starting point, nudged it a little, and stopped at the first machine that cleared the bar. Not the best machine. The first acceptable one.

The surrogate changes the economics of that search completely. When one physics evaluation drops from hours to microseconds, you stop nudging and start hunting. You wrap the fast model in an optimizer that roams the whole design space, evaluating millions of candidate machines, and it finds not the first acceptable point but the genuinely best one — the operating point that sits deepest inside the feasible region, farthest from every limit, cheapest to run. This is the sense in which fusion has an optimization code to crack: the physics tells you which machines are possible, but the optimization tells you which possible machine is best, and you cannot ask that second question at all until each answer is cheap.

We ran exactly this experiment on the program's own design engine — a verified Monte-Carlo model that samples the feasibility of a candidate machine across three hundred thousand points, and that reproduces its feasibility counts bit-for-bit from a single seed, so the search is auditable and not a black box. A Bayesian-optimization surrogate wrapped around that engine reached the optimum with a genuine 3.8-fold reduction in the number of evaluations a random search would have needed. I state that number carefully, because a naïve comparison against brute force would have let me quote something far larger and far less honest — most of brute force's cost is its own inefficiency, not the optimizer's cleverness, and I will not claim credit for a baseline's waste. Against a fair random-search baseline, 3.8× is the real, defensible speedup, and 3.8× is what I report.

The physics tells you which machines are possible; the optimization tells you which possible machine is best; and you cannot even ask that second question until every answer is cheap. This is why I insist that the design of the two machines and the intelligence that runs them are not two projects but one. The same surrogate that lets an optimizer find the best breeder in an afternoon is the surrogate that, deployed in the loop, lets the controller anticipate that breeder's plasma fifty milliseconds ahead. The exact physics is the teacher; the surrogate is the student that inherits the teacher's accuracy and the loop's speed; and once you have that student, you can spend it two ways — to find the machine and to run it. Cracking the optimization code was never about a single clever algorithm. It was about making the expensive question cheap enough to ask a million times.

Seeing trouble coming

Two more results, both about the oldest survival skill there is: seeing danger before it arrives. A gazelle that senses the lion a half-second early lives; the machine that senses its own catastrophe a few milliseconds early does too.

The first is disruption prediction. A disruption is the plasma's sudden, total collapse — an abrupt loss of confinement that hurls everything it was holding into the walls at once. Deep-learning models have predicted disruptions across machines for years; that is established. What we built is an ensemble anomaly detector that, on twin-synthetic pulses anchored to the real operating space of an existing spherical tokamak, reached an AUC of 0.990 with a false-alarm rate of four percent.

That number deserves translation, because "AUC" is a piece of jargon that hides a genuinely useful idea.

AUC 0.990: pick a real disruption and a calm moment at random, and 99 times out of 100 the model rates the disruption as the more dangerous of the two.

That is what area-under-the-curve means, concretely. It is the probability that the model correctly ranks a true danger above a false one. A perfect predictor scores 1.0; a coin flip scores 0.5; 0.990 means the model almost never confuses a disruption with a quiet plasma. And here again the honesty: the model's warning time missed our target — we wanted 30 milliseconds of lead and the median was 22.3, with fewer than a third of events clearing the full 30. So we did not paper over it with a better average. We handled it architecturally: an out-of-distribution layer that recognizes disruption types the model has never seen — an impurity influx, a vertical displacement — and, instead of issuing a confident-but-wrong command, abstains and hands the machine to the hardware failsafe. On those unseen classes, that handoff cut the missed-alarm fraction from about 0.9 to zero. The model's humility, wired into the architecture, is safer than the model's confidence. A predictor that knows the difference between "this is safe" and "I have never seen this" is worth more than a slightly more accurate predictor that cannot tell the two apart.

The second is the magnets. The breeder and burner both run on high-temperature REBCO superconductor at fields up to nearly 27 tesla, and a superconducting magnet that begins to "quench" — to lose its superconductivity in a spreading normal zone — can destroy itself if the quench is caught late. The traditional detector watches for a voltage rise across the coil terminals. In these no-insulation coils the normal zone spreads slowly, so terminal voltage is a late signal — it gave, in our twin, about 2.6 milliseconds of warning. We fused two other channels instead: the mechanical strain measured by fiber-optic sensors woven into the winding, and the coil's magnetization signature. The fused precursor gave 47 milliseconds of warning for the same event, at an AUC of 0.9998 and a false-alarm rate of 2.4 percent.

Let me make forty-seven-versus-two-and-a-half concrete, because it is the difference between an inconvenience and a catastrophe. When a magnet quenches, the energy stored in its field has to go somewhere. If you know early, you fire the dump circuits and discharge that energy gracefully, spread over the whole coil, and the magnet lives to run again. If you know late, the energy deposits into the small normal zone that started the quench, a spot heats to destruction, and you are looking at months of repair and a plant sitting idle. Terminal voltage, at 2.6 milliseconds, is often too late to choose the graceful path. Forty-seven milliseconds is not — the difference, operationally, between a magnet you replace and a magnet you merely reset.

The same magnet twin does two more useful things worth naming. Fed each coil's as-built measured data rather than a worst-case assumption, it recovered thirty percent more usable current density from every coil — because worst-case derating throws away margin that the real, measured coil actually has, and it keeps, rather than hides, the minority of coils where the measured margin is worse. And it computes a per-turn pre-load — an engineered residual compression, turn by turn — that brings the operating strain on all 82 turns of a coil to 0.017 percent, comfortably inside the 0.40 percent limit, instead of letting strain peak dangerously at the inner turns. Measured data, used honestly, is worth more than conservative assumptions used fearfully.

A quench, millisecond by millisecond

Set two clocks running on the same quenching magnet, and you will understand why forty-seven versus two-and-a-half is not a marginal improvement but a change of category — the difference between a prediction that can drive an action and a prediction that arrives after the action is already too late.

Somewhere in a high-field REBCO coil, a tiny region gives up its superconductivity and goes normal — resistive. Perhaps a turn shifted a few microns under the Lorentz load; perhaps a flaw in the tape finally mattered. A normal zone is born, and it begins to spread. In a no-insulation coil it spreads slowly and quietly, which is a mercy for the coil's robustness and a curse for the traditional detector, because a slow-spreading normal zone raises almost no voltage across the terminals until it is large. But it is not silent everywhere. The fiber-optic strain sensor woven into the winding feels the local mechanical signature of the newborn zone, and the coil's magnetization signature begins to shift as current redistributes around the resistive spot. The fused precursor — strain and magnetization together — crosses its threshold and raises the alarm. Call that instant t = 0. On this clock, the controller has 47 milliseconds of runway before the quench becomes unsurvivable.

Now start the second clock, the traditional one. The terminal-voltage detector feels nothing yet, because the normal zone is still too small to build a voltage. It will keep feeling nothing for another 44.4 milliseconds. Only at t = 44.4 ms does the spreading zone finally raise enough voltage to trip the classical detector — leaving just 2.6 milliseconds before the point of no return. Same magnet, same quench, two detectors: one shouts at t = 0, the other whispers at t = 44.4.

What those extra milliseconds buy is a choice. With 47 milliseconds in hand, the controller can take the graceful path. It begins to ramp the transport current down, and it arms and fires the dump circuits — the resistors and switches whose job is to pull the enormous energy stored in the magnetic field out of the coil and dissipate it, spread evenly across the whole winding rather than concentrated at one point. The stored energy leaves the coil in an orderly discharge. The normal zone, starved of the current that fed it, cools and never runs away. The magnet is reset, checked, and run again. Nothing is destroyed. Operationally, this is a pause, not a wound.

Run the same event on the 2.6-millisecond clock and the choice is gone. Two and a half milliseconds is often too little to ramp and dump gracefully, so the field's stored energy has nowhere orderly to go. It deposits into the small normal zone that started it all, the spot heats catastrophically, and a coil that cost months to wind is destroyed at the one point where the quench began. The plant then sits idle for the months it takes to build and install a replacement.

This is why the precursor is an economic instrument every bit as much as a safety one. A magnet you reset costs you an afternoon; a magnet you replace costs you a quarter of downtime, and downtime is a direct assault on the capacity factor that sets the price of every megawatt-hour. The prediction and the action are a single mechanism: the forty-seven-millisecond warning exists precisely so that the dump circuits can fire on the graceful side of the line, and the whole value of seeing early is that it lets you act gently.

Knowing what it does not know

Two properties separate a controller a regulator will license from a demonstration that merely works on a good day. One is that it fences its own intelligence — the clamp and the barrier function above. The other is quieter and just as important: it has to know, at every instant, how much to trust its own numbers, and it has to keep running when its senses fail. A confident controller that is confidently wrong is more dangerous than a cautious one that is right about its own doubt.

Start with the doubt. Every prediction the surrogates emit carries an uncertainty — a stated interval within which the true value is claimed to lie — and a stated interval is worthless unless it is honest. If a model says "I am 90 percent sure the answer is in this band," then across many predictions the truth had better fall inside that band about 90 percent of the time, no more and no less. A model whose 90-percent bands catch the truth only 60 percent of the time is not cautious; it is lying, and a safety case built on its intervals is built on sand. So we calibrate the intervals themselves, using a conformal method that adjusts the bands until their stated confidence matches their measured hit rate. On our surrogates the calibrated coverage lands between 0.88 and 0.90 against a 0.90 target — close, honest, and — the part I insist on reporting — slightly over-confident in the far tail, where the rare, extreme events live. We keep that tail over-confidence on the record rather than smoothing it away, because the tail is exactly where a fusion plant gets hurt, and a reader deserves to know the one place our uncertainty estimate is weakest.

Now the failing senses. A fusion plant is instrumented by dozens of diagnostic channels, and diagnostics die — a fiber darkens under neutron flux, a cable picks up noise, a probe simply stops reporting. A brittle controller trips the whole plant the instant a channel drops, which is a catastrophe for uptime. So we taught the twin to see through a missing sensor. A graph neural network — a model that understands how the diagnostics are physically wired to one another, which channel sits next to which — reconstructs a dropped signal from its surviving neighbors at roughly twice the accuracy of naive interpolation between them. That factor of two is not a bragging number; it is a budget. It defines, quantitatively, how many sensors the plant is allowed to lose and keep running inside a certified degraded-state envelope, and — kept honestly — the reconstruction does not reach our stricter target at every level of channel loss, so the envelope is drawn where the model earns it, not where we wish it were. A plant that keeps producing power with three sensors down, inside a fence it can prove it is still behind, has a capacity factor a plant that trips on the first dropout can only dream of.

De-circularization: proving the twin is not just grading its own homework

There is an objection a careful reader should already be forming, and I want to meet it head-on. Every number above lives on a digital twin. What stops a twin from being a flattering mirror — a simulator that validates the simulator, a model that agrees with itself because it was built to? Nothing, unless you go looking for the circularity on purpose. So we did, two independent ways. First, we checked the twin's equilibrium against an entirely separate, open-source equilibrium solver written by a different community for a different purpose, and the fields agreed to within 2.66 percent — with one axis-flux discrepancy we keep as a characterized failure mode rather than sand off. By that check, our internal "circularity index" roughly halved. Second, we benchmarked the twin's magnet, materials, and thermomechanics assumptions against the published engineering design basis of the largest international tokamak project, tagging each of nineteen assumptions as inside that envelope, deliberately outside it, or having no basis in it at all. Some of our choices — high-temperature superconductor at high field and strain — are outside that reference by design, because it uses a different conductor, and we label them so rather than imply endorsement. It is an engineering-basis benchmark, not proof from an operating plasma, and I say so — but it is the difference between a twin that only talks to itself and one forced to answer to an outside authority.

Why control is economics

It would be easy to file everything in this chapter under "safety" and move on. That would miss the point. Reach back to the spine of this book — the second forty, forty dollars per megawatt-hour. The control system is not a cost center that protects the revenue. For a fusion plant, the control system is a large part of the revenue.

Here is why. The dominant driver of the levelized cost of any capital-heavy generator — fusion, fission, anything you build from steel and superconductor — is not the fuel and it is not the operating staff. It is the capacity factor: what fraction of the year the machine is actually producing. A plant that runs 95 percent of the time and a plant that runs 70 percent of the time have wildly different costs per megawatt-hour from the same hardware. Every unplanned trip, every disruption that damages a wall, every magnet quench caught too late and repaired over months, is a direct assault on that number.

So a predictive shadow that anticipates off-normal events before they trip the plant, a disruption predictor that buys time to mitigate, a quench precursor that turns a magnet-destroying event into a routine discharge, a maintenance loop that replaces components against modeled fatigue rather than fixed calendar intervals — every one of these is a lever on capacity factor, and therefore a lever on price. There are more. The predictive isotope-balancing loop that holds the fuel mix on its lowest-neutron trajectory cut the fuel-mix tracking error more than thirteenfold against an open-loop baseline — and a tighter fuel mix means less neutron damage to the walls, which again is uptime. Because the burner produces its power on a direct-current bus, the same twin that keeps the plasma safe also knows, instant to instant, exactly what the machine can deliver — which is precisely the knowledge you need to bid firm power into a grid market. And the state-reconstruction that lets the plant keep running with failed sensors, and the operator-training that happens on the twin instead of the real machine, reduce the specialized-staffing burden that would otherwise make a fleet of small reactors uneconomic to run. Uptime is price. Safety is price. The machine that controls the machine is, in the end, one of the machines that hits the forty-dollar line.

That roadmap deserves one clarification, because "quantum" gets attached to fusion far too loosely. Of the three tiers it shows, the middle one — quantum sensing — is the one that touches the plant soonest and most concretely. Superconducting-loop magnetometers are already mature enough to sit in fusion diagnostics; solid-state diamond sensors and atomic magnetometers are climbing behind them. The fusion-specific point is not the sensor itself but the coupling: a sharper measurement of the magnetic field tightens the boundary condition the equilibrium reconstruction depends on, which lowers the state-estimation error the whole control stack inherits. Sensing sharpens the state the AI consumes today; computation calibrates the models offline tomorrow; neither one is ever allowed inside the fast loop. Holding those three tiers strictly apart — and refusing to let the far-future tier borrow credibility for the present — is itself part of the honesty this chapter is built on.

What this chapter is, and is not

Let me close with the disclosure that governs everything above, because it is the same disclosure that runs through this whole book. Kronos operates no fusion plant. Every number in this chapter comes from a physics-based digital twin, from public data, or from simulation, and each is tagged with its provenance in the published paper. The three thousand caught violations, the 7475× calibration, the 47-millisecond warning, the 0.990 AUC, the certified safety envelope, and the 2.5-percent miss — all of it lives on the twin, not on a burning plasma, and I say so plainly.

That is not a hedge. It is the honest sequence, the only sequence that has ever ended in a working machine: you prove the control and certification methods in simulation first, and then you earn the right to touch hardware — never the other way around. The decade of solved, published physics behind the two machines is the bedrock. What this chapter describes is the intelligence that will stand on it — fast enough to act inside a microsecond, contained enough to satisfy a regulator, honest enough to tell you exactly which target it missed and by how much. For all of human history, holding a star has been the exclusive privilege of gravity and the vacuum of space. When the first breeder wakes at the turn of the decade, a mind built to share that privilege will already be waiting for it — rehearsed ten thousand times against its digital ghost, proven in simulation to keep the star inside the fence. That is what it takes to bring a piece of the cosmos down to Earth and make it behave.

Quantum, Honestly

There are two words in modern science that can make an audience lean forward before you finish the sentence: fusion and quantum. Put them together and you have written the most seductive headline of the century — the two great physics revolutions of our age, joined at last, one computing the other into existence. In the 2024 version of this book, I wrote that headline. I let the word quantum do far more work than it had earned. I said, in effect, that a new kind of computer would crack the equations of the plasma the way a quantum machine is supposed to crack everything else, and that this was part of why our road to fusion would run faster than the field's. It was the most thrilling sentence in the chapter. It was also the least defensible one. Two years of actually grinding through the resource estimates — not gesturing at them, doing them, digit by digit — have taught me exactly where quantum technology helps these machines and exactly where it does not, and the honest map bears little resemblance to the one I drew before. This chapter is the correction. I would rather you catch me revising a claim than watch me never dare to test one.

The correction has a clean structure, and I will give it to you at the top so nothing is buried. There are two technologies that both get called "quantum," and they are on opposite sides of the honesty line. Quantum computing offers our problem no useful advantage this decade — the numbers are not close, and I will show you why. Quantum sensing is genuinely near and genuinely useful — it is the deployable quantum story, and it belongs to diagnostics, not to computation. Conflating the two is how a serious field talks itself into hype. Separating them is how it earns back trust.

The three tiers, held strictly apart

Discipline, in a field this intoxicating, is everything. When the company's engineers rebuilt the control and computation architecture for the two machines — the breeder Hyperion and the tandem-mirror burner — we forced ourselves to sort every technology we touch into one of three readiness tiers, and then we made a vow: never, under any temptation, let a claim slide from a lower tier into a higher one. That single rule is the firewall between a science and a sales pitch.

The first tier is physics-informed machine learning, deployable now, inside the control loop, provided its error is bounded and a deterministic clamp catches anything out of bounds. That is the subject of the AI chapter, and it is working today with hard numbers behind it.

The second tier is quantum sensing, near-term, living in the diagnostics layer — sharpening the measurement of the plasma's state that the AI then consumes. Not computing anything; measuring something, better.

The third tier is quantum computation, offline only — a calibration tier with, on our own estimates, no crossover against classical methods this decade. It does not touch the plant. It does not run inside any control loop. If it ever helps, it helps between shots, computing a high-fidelity closure that gets folded into a classical model through a gate that re-proves the machine is still safe before the new number is allowed to matter.

The discipline is the whole point. A sentence like "a quantum computer controls the plasma" is not optimistic — it is physically false, and I have retired it. A sentence like "quantum-computed closures reduce our surrogate error offline, with an explicit resource estimate and a dated crossover" is testable. So we tested it. The test came back negative for this decade, and printing that negative is the reason to believe everything else in this book.

Why quantum computing does not help — yet

Here is the part I got wrong, stated as plainly as I know how to state it.

The promise of quantum computing is one of the most genuinely astonishing ideas in the history of physics: harness the strange arithmetic of superposition and entanglement, and a machine could explore an exponential thicket of possibilities all at once, solving in an afternoon problems that would outlast the universe on any ordinary computer. That promise is real — for the right problems. The whole question is whether our problems are the right ones. To model or reconstruct a plasma you spend most of your computer time solving a small number of mathematical kernels over and over. Three of them matter most: the equilibrium solve (given the coils and currents, what shape does the plasma settle into?), the kinetic or Vlasov solve (how does the swarm of particles evolve in the six-dimensional space of position and velocity?), and the materials solve (how does the reactor wall's chemistry change under a fusion neutron bombardment?). The hope — my hope, when I first wrote this — was that a quantum computer would do one or more of these so much faster than a classical computer that the whole design-and-control problem would open up.

To check the hope honestly you cannot wave at "quantum speedup." You have to write down a specific fault-tolerant architecture — a surface-code machine with a stated physical error rate, code distance, cycle time, and a stated number of the "factories" that manufacture the expensive quantum operations — and then count. The expensive operation, the one that dominates the cost, is called a T-gate. So you count T-gates. Every assumption sits in a spreadsheet column, so no number is narrated into being; each one is derived.

We counted, for all three kernels, and none of them crosses over into quantum advantage this decade under any plausible assumption in the ranges we swept. The kinetic kernel needs roughly 130 logical qubits and about 1.3 × 10¹³ T-gates and still loses on wall-clock time to the classical gyrokinetic codes we already run. The materials kernel is the closest to useful — it lands within an order of magnitude of a published fault-tolerant chemistry estimate, which is actually how we validated that our cost model was not lying to us. And the equilibrium solve, the most everyday calculation of the three, produced the number that ended the argument.

The most defensible thing I can say about quantum computing and fusion is a date, not a promise. Not "it won't help" — "here is the problem, the algorithm, and the earliest year the hardware could possibly earn its place."

A number, translated. The equilibrium linear solve — once you honestly count the cost of loading the problem into the quantum computer and reading a useful answer back out — needs about 1.8 × 10¹⁷ T-gates. That read-in and read-out penalty is the killer, and it is the part hand-wavy treatments quietly drop; it erases the asymptotic speedup that made quantum linear algebra sound magical in the first place. What does 1.8 × 10¹⁷ mean in human terms? Imagine a fault-tolerant machine that could execute a million T-gates every second — a rate wildly beyond anything error-corrected hardware has ever demonstrated. At that rate, a single equilibrium solve would take about 1.8 × 10¹¹ seconds, which is roughly 5,700 years. And the control system needs a fresh equilibrium reconstruction many times per second, for the entire pulse. This is not a gap you close with a better compiler or one more hardware generation. It is astronomically beyond the near term, and it is the honest reason quantum linear algebra does not touch this problem today.

How you actually count. I want to be transparent about where a number like 1.8 × 10¹⁷ comes from, because a resource estimate that cannot be inspected is just a bigger promise. We fix a single cost model and apply it to all three kernels without adjustment. It assumes a specific kind of error-corrected machine — a surface-code architecture — with a stated physical error rate, a stated code distance (how many physical qubits are braided together to protect one logical qubit), a stated cycle time, and a stated number of the "factories" that manufacture the expensive T-gates. From those inputs, four outputs follow by arithmetic: the number of logical qubits, the number of T-gates, the depth of the circuit, and the wall-clock time. Every one of those assumptions lives in its own column of a spreadsheet, so no number is narrated into being — each is derived, and each can be swept across a plausible range to see whether the conclusion is fragile. It is not. Across every combination in the ranges we swept, no kernel crosses over this decade.

The three kernels are worth separating, because they fail for three different reasons, and the reasons are instructive.

  • The kinetic (Vlasov) kernel is limited by the mathematical machinery you need to make a quantum computer handle it at all. The collision physics is nonlinear, and a quantum computer's native operations are linear, so you first lift the problem into a much larger linear space — a Carleman tower — and that lifting multiplies the qubit register. The result: about 130 logical qubits and roughly 1.3 × 10¹³ T-gates, and even then it loses on wall-clock to the classical gyrokinetic codes we already run today.
  • The equilibrium linear solve is the cautionary tale of the three, because on paper it is where quantum linear algebra promises the most, and in practice it is where the promise evaporates most completely. The famous quantum speedup for solving linear systems is real inside the machine — but you have to load the problem in and read a useful answer out, and both of those cost dearly. Preparing the input state and extracting a meaningful functional of the solution, rather than a single lucky amplitude, erases the asymptotic advantage and drives the T-count to 1.8 × 10¹⁷. That read-in/read-out penalty is the part hand-wavy treatments quietly drop.
  • The materials kernel is the closest to useful, and it plays a special role: it lands within an order of magnitude of a published fault-tolerant chemistry estimate for a comparable problem. That agreement is not a result about materials — it is how we checked that our whole cost model was not lying to us. If our independent count of a problem someone else has costed agrees with theirs, the model is calibrated, and its verdict on the other two kernels can be trusted.
The read-in and read-out penalty is where quantum linear algebra dies for this problem. The speedup is real inside the box. Getting the question in and the answer out is what costs 5,700 years.

I want to be careful about what that estimate is and is not. It is a negative result for this decade. It is not a claim that quantum computation is irrelevant to fusion forever. Three fusion problems are classically hard in a deep, structural way — first-principles turbulent transport across a whole device over long times; plasma-and-wall evolution under neutron irradiation, which is a strongly-correlated quantum-chemistry problem exactly where our engineering margins are thinnest; and the coupled kinetic-electromagnetic behavior near the edge of stability, where the answer you need is a small difference between large, noisy quantities. For each of these, a fault-tolerant quantum computer genuinely changes the asymptotic cost. So the honest posture is not "quantum will never help." It is: here is the specific problem, the specific algorithm, the logical-qubit and error-rate threshold it demands, and therefore the earliest defensible date. A roadmap, with thresholds on it — not a miracle on the loop.

Our variational proof-of-concept tells the same story in miniature, and it is worth watching the gap open. A variational algorithm is one of the leading candidates for getting useful chemistry out of near-term, not-yet-fault-tolerant hardware, so it is the fairest test of the optimistic case. On an idealized statevector simulator — a perfect, noiseless machine that exists only in software — it reaches chemical accuracy, which is genuinely encouraging and is the number an optimist would quote and stop. But a real quantum processor is not noiseless; every gate leaks a little error, and those errors compound. Switch on a realistic model of that device noise and the same algorithm misses chemical accuracy by somewhere between fourteen and thirteen hundred times, depending on the problem. That factor between the clean simulator and the noisy one is the scale wall — the distance between what quantum computing can do in principle and what today's hardware can do in fact. And I have to be scrupulous here: this is simulator-only work. We modeled the noise; we did not run on cloud quantum hardware, and I will not let a careful reader come away thinking we did.

Quantum computing's actual, useful job: offline calibration

Retiring a false claim is only half of honesty. The other half is finding the true thing that was hiding underneath it. There is one, and it is quietly powerful.

If a high-fidelity closure ever can be computed — classically today, or by a quantum computer on the dated roadmap above — the right way to use it is not to put it in the control loop. It is to use it as a rare, expensive anchor that calibrates a cheap, fast classical surrogate the loop actually runs. This is the mechanism at the heart of our architecture, and it is measurable. Inject a handful of high-fidelity closure anchors into a control surrogate and its error drops by up to roughly seventeen-hundred-fold on a chemistry benchmark, reaching chemical accuracy with as few as five anchors. Crucially, we demonstrated this with a classical full-configuration-interaction calculation standing in for the future quantum-computed closure — so it is a demonstration of the mechanism, honestly, not a demonstration of quantum advantage sneaking in the back door.

And the reason I trust this mechanism is that it is not a chemistry trick — it transfers. The same lever we pulled on the chemistry benchmark, we pulled on two problems that have nothing to do with molecules. On a plasma-transport closure — the physics of how heat leaks across the confined plasma — eight high-fidelity anchors cut the surrogate's error by 36.8-fold, beating the best reduced-physics model by nearly a factor of ten. On the magnet twin — the strain in a superconducting coil under load — the same lever reached up to three orders of magnitude, a factor of 7475 at its strongest. Three domains as different as chemistry, turbulent heat transport, and structural mechanics, and one mechanism improves all three. That is what convinces me it is real rather than a coincidence of one lucky benchmark: a domain-specific fluke does not survive being carried into two unrelated fields. A general mechanism does. So when I say quantum computing's honest job is to be an anchor factory, I am not speculating about a role it might one day play — I am describing a pipeline that already works, waiting only for a better source of anchors.

That reframing is what makes the architecture forward-compatible with quantum hardware without betting the plant on it. The day a machine capable of one of those three closures exists, its output enters our plant only as an offline, provenance-gated calibration anchor — admitted through a gate that re-proves the safety invariant before the new number is allowed to change a single actuator command — and never as an in-loop dependency. Quantum computing earns its place at the design-and-calibration layer, on named problems, on a dated schedule. That is the whole, honest thesis, and it is a far smaller and far truer claim than the one I made before.

The quantum win that is real today — and is not a quantum computer

Now for the twist in the story — the win that is real today, hiding in plain sight amid all this walking-back. It turns out you do not need to build the quantum computer to harvest one of quantum physics' deepest insights. You only need to think the way the quantum theorists learned to think. This is a quantum-inspired classical method — no dilution refrigerator, no logical qubits, no fault-tolerant hardware anywhere in sight — and it works on today's machines.

The kinetic kernel — the six-dimensional particle problem — can be attacked with a technique borrowed from quantum many-body physics called a matrix-product state, or tensor network. The idea is worth unpacking, because it is the single best illustration of what "quantum-inspired" honestly means. When physicists first tried to simulate quantum systems on classical computers, they hit a wall: the mathematical object describing a many-particle quantum state grows exponentially with the number of particles, and it swamps any machine almost immediately. The escape was the realization that most of that object is redundant — real physical states do not use all their theoretical correlations, only a structured few. A matrix-product state is a way of storing only the correlations that actually matter, throwing away the rest in a controlled way. The control knob is a single number, the bond dimension d: crank it up and you keep more correlation and pay more; turn it down and you approximate more crudely and pay less. It is a dial that trades accuracy for cost, and you set it exactly as high as the physics demands and no higher.

Applied to the kinetic kernel, the dial tells an honest story. At small bond dimension — d = 3, d = 4 — the classical brute-force methods still win, and we kept that result rather than hiding it, because a benchmark that only reports the settings where you win is not a benchmark. But the picture inverts as the physics gets richer. At d = 6 the tensor-network solver beats the classical baseline by about 3.9 times at fixed cost; at d = 7 by 21.2 times; and — this is the part that matters — at d ≥ 10 it is the only feasible method at all. Beyond that bond dimension the classical baseline simply cannot fit in the machine; the tensor network still can. We validated it to machine precision, one part in 10¹⁵, against exact diagonalization on the cases small enough to check both ways, so the speed did not come at the price of correctness. It is a benchmark that bounds the near-term quantum claim from below — anything a real quantum computer eventually does to this kernel has to beat this, not the naïve baseline — and the underlying approach is published, not invented here. The lesson is worth keeping: the useful "quantum" in fusion computing this decade is a way of thinking, imported into classical code — not a quantum processor humming in a dilution refrigerator.

Quantum sensing: the deployable quantum story

Now the technology that is genuinely, unglamorously near — the quantum revolution that will actually walk through the door of a fusion plant this decade. When people hear "quantum" and "fusion" in the same breath and get excited, this is what they should be excited about, and almost nobody is, because it does not come with the science-fiction glow of a quantum computer dissolving the equations of the plasma. What it does is humbler and, for us, far more useful. It measures a magnetic field. That is all. But it measures the field absolutely — anchored to a constant of nature that cannot drift, cannot age, cannot be argued with — and that unwavering honesty is worth more to these machines than any amount of raw sensitivity.

A quantum magnetometer reads a magnetic field by watching what the field does to the quantum states of atoms or defects. The best-known kind, the nitrogen-vacancy or NV center, is an atomic-scale flaw in a diamond whose energy levels split apart in proportion to the field. You read the field as a frequency — and a frequency is tied to a fundamental constant of nature, the electron gyromagnetic ratio, γₑ ≈ 28.03 GHz per tesla. That is the magic, and it is a subtle magic.

Here is the counterintuitive part, and it is the finding that reorganized how I think about sensing in our machines. The femtotesla sensitivities that make quantum magnetometers famous are irrelevant inside a tokamak. Our fields are measured in teslas — eight teslas on axis in Hyperion. That is a trillion to a thousand-trillion times larger than the sensor's noise floor. Quantum sensing does not win on sensitivity here; there is nothing subtle to detect. If it wins, it wins on something else entirely.

It is worth dwelling on why, because the whole excitement around quantum metrology is about sensitivity, and I am telling you sensitivity is the wrong axis for this job. The reason quantum sensors can be so exquisitely sensitive is a scaling law. A conventional measurement that averages N independent quantum probes beats down its noise as one over the square root of N — the shot-noise limit, the same law of averages that governs a political poll. Entangle those probes first, and in principle the noise falls as one over N itself — the Heisenberg limit, quadratically better. That quadratic is the crown jewel of quantum sensing, and it is genuinely revolutionary for measuring things that are almost too faint to detect: a single neuron's magnetic whisper, a gravitational wave, a trace of a molecule.

``` Two ways precision improves with N probes:

shot-noise limit δB ∝ 1 / √N (independent probes)

Heisenberg limit δB ∝ 1 / N (entangled probes)

In a tokamak the field is ~8 T and the sensor floor is ~femtotesla — fifteen orders of magnitude of headroom. Neither scaling law is the binding constraint. Sensitivity is not the problem we have. ```

Hold those two scaling laws up against the numbers and the conclusion is unavoidable. When the quantity you are measuring is fifteen orders of magnitude above your noise floor, it does not matter whether your noise falls as one over root-N or one over N; you have precision to burn either way. The heroic quantum sensitivity is spent on a problem we do not have. So if a quantum magnetometer is going to earn a place in one of our machines, it has to earn it on a completely different property — and it does.

What a frequency reference buys you. The conventional way to measure a tokamak's field is with inductive pickup coils that measure the rate of change of the field and then integrate it up over time. Integrators are excellent — abundant signal, huge bandwidth, radiation-hard cabling — but they have one deep weakness: over a long pulse they drift. And in a neutron field the drift is not merely electronic. The radiation itself injects spurious voltages directly into the sensor cabling (the effect has an ungainly name, radiation-induced electromotive force) that corrupt the integrated field over a long shot. A quantum magnetometer does not integrate anything. It reports an absolute frequency tied to a constant of nature. It cannot accumulate that drift because there is nothing accumulating. That is the gap it fills — not sensitivity, but absolute, drift-immune, self-calibrating accuracy over a long pulse. As a bonus, a single NV center reports its own temperature at the same time, from a separate, known frequency shift of −74 kHz per kelvin — a co-located field-and-temperature reading with no classical analogue.

Three modalities anchor this tier, and they sort cleanly by maturity. The superconducting-loop magnetometer — the SQUID — is the most established; it already sits in fusion diagnostics, offers the highest raw sensitivity, and pays for it with cryogenics and a fussy intolerance of stray field. The nitrogen-vacancy diamond is the most promising for actually living inside a vessel: it is solid-state, it works from cryogenic temperatures all the way to room temperature, and it needs no exotic support — but its demonstrated sensitivity trails the SQUID and, as I am about to explain, its survival in a neutron field is the open question that decides everything. The atomic, optically-pumped magnetometers sit in between. And there is a second axis besides maturity that matters just as much and gets forgotten: bandwidth. A sensor that cannot report a fresh reading inside the control system's latency band is, by definition, an offline-analysis instrument no matter how sensitive it is — it cannot enter the loop, because the loop has already moved on by the time it answers. So we sort every modality twice: by how mature it is, and by whether it is fast enough to be in the loop or only fast enough to inform the analysis afterward.

I have to be equally honest about what stands in the way, because this is a scoping result, not a finished diagnostic. The other famous quantum magnetometers are ruled out at the source: the ultra-sensitive atomic (SERF) magnetometer only works in a near-zero field and is simply dead at eight teslas, and a SQUID is destroyed by flux trapping in any multi-tesla stray field and needs cryogenics besides. That leaves the NV diamond, and the NV diamond faces a radiation problem that decides everything. Using our own neutron-transport fluence maps, an unshielded NV sensor at the first wall — exactly where an in-vessel field measurement would be most valuable — has a functional life on the order of a single day, on our assumed degradation threshold. It only reaches a multi-year life behind sixty centimeters of shielding or fully outside the vessel — which is precisely where the conventional magnetics already sit, and where the drift advantage, while still real, is least urgent. Radiation pushes the quantum sensor toward the one place its unique advantage matters least. And I will flag the single largest uncertainty rather than smooth it over: the fluence at which an NV center actually stops working under a fusion neutron spectrum is, to the best of the public record, unmeasured. It is an assumption in our study, and the decisive experiment that would settle it has not been done. A fusion-qualified NV magnetic diagnostic is, honestly, at technology-readiness level two to three — a bench program, not a product.

So the deployable quantum story is real but modest, and I would rather give you the modest true version. Quantum sensing's genuine, non-redundant contribution to these machines is an absolute, drift-immune, steady-state magnetic reference — most likely mounted outside the vessel — that anchors the long-pulse drift of the conventional coils and feeds a cleaner boundary condition into the equilibrium reconstruction the AI consumes. It is a complement that closes the one real weakness of an otherwise superb classical diagnostic set. It is not a replacement, and it is not a revolution. It is a good, honest instrument with a hard radiation problem still to solve.

Why I am telling you this

I could have quietly dropped the quantum-computing claim this time and hoped no one who read the earlier version noticed. That is the normal move. I am not making it, for a reason that goes beyond this one chapter.

A book like this asks you to believe a great many numbers you cannot personally check — the gain, the field, the neutron balance, the timeline. You have every right to ask why you should. My answer is the same one I gave when I retired the phrase "net gain in 2027" and replaced it with the truth that 2027 is when construction begins: I would rather show you a corrected claim than a comfortable one. The quantum-computing walk-back is the cleanest example I have. We ran the estimate, the estimate said no crossover this decade, and so the claim is gone — reframed into the smaller, truer role it actually plays. A field, and a founder, willing to say this part of my last book was too optimistic has, I think, earned the standing to be believed on the parts that held.

So let this chapter stand as the proof of the whole book's method. The quantum honesty is not a crack in the story. It is the load-bearing beam holding the story up. We live in an age drunk on the word "quantum," an age that will attach it to anything to make it shimmer — and it would have cost me nothing to let fusion shimmer along with the rest. I chose the harder, truer thing. Everything else in these pages — the gain, the fields, the neutron balance, the forty-year horizon — asks for your trust, and here is the collateral I put down for it: when the numbers contradicted my enthusiasm, I printed the numbers. A field willing to do that is a field you can follow all the way to a star.

The Twin: Simulating a Machine Before We Build It

Four centuries ago, an astronomer could predict an eclipse to the minute but could not build the heavens he was charting. We have inverted that ancient bargain. Today we can build a star's engine in a computer — every field line, every neutron, every turn of superconducting tape — years before we pour its foundations. There is a particular kind of nerve required to publish the full design of a power plant you have not built, cannot yet build, and will not begin building until construction breaks ground in 2027. The whole argument of this book is that the physics is solved — gain solved, not scaled — and that the two machines are reproducible on paper by anyone willing to check the math. But a design on paper carries a quiet, load-bearing assumption beneath every number: that the real machine, once welded together from steel and superconductor and chilled to within a few degrees of absolute zero, will actually behave the way the equations swear it will. Fusion history is a graveyard of designs that were flawless on paper and wrong in the vessel. So the honest question is not "is the design correct?" It is the harder one: "how do you wring the risk out of a machine before a single component of it exists?" This chapter is about the answer — a digital twin, and the simulation program that gives that twin teeth sharp enough to bite its own maker.

"Digital twin" is one of the most abused phrases in modern engineering — easy to say, brutally hard to earn. Anyone can build a model that nods along with the design it was born from. That is not a twin. It is a mirror, and a mirror tells you nothing you did not already believe. A twin earns the name only when it is faithful enough to surprise you — faithful enough to reproduce a real experiment it was never shown, and then to turn around and reveal something about your own machine you never put in by hand. The difference between a mirror and a twin is the difference between flattery and a second opinion, and only one of them can save your life. That distinction — between a model that flatters the design and a model that could have proven it wrong — is the whole discipline of this chapter. It is also the reason the program is built the way it is, and the reason I will spend as much time on what did not work as on what did.

The gate is confinement

Reach back to the first of the three forties — Q40, the physics: forty times more fusion energy out than the energy we spend to hold the plasma. The breeder, Hyperion, is a compact spherical tokamak with a major radius of just 1.2 metres, an aspect ratio of 2.5, elongation 2.0, and 8 tesla on axis. Its published scientific gain is Q_sci ≈ 3.076 — modest, deliberately so, because Hyperion's near-term business is making fuel, not power. But whether it hits even that number depends on one thing above all others, and it is not a number you can read off a blueprint. It is how fast heat leaks out of the plasma.

Consider the sheer violence of the gradient we are asking this machine to hold. A fusion plasma is a hundred million degrees at its heart and merely warm at the wall a few centimetres away — the steepest temperature cliff anywhere in the solar system this side of a supernova. Nature loathes a gradient like that. Heat claws its way down the slope and toward the exit, and the rate at which it escapes — the turbulent transport — sets the confinement time. Confinement time is the thin line dividing a machine that ignites from a machine that merely glows and dies. Here is the uncomfortable part: turbulent transport is not something you can calculate with a formula. It emerges from the plasma tearing itself into a froth of microscopic eddies, driven by instabilities with names like the ion-temperature-gradient mode, and the only way to compute it from first principles is to simulate the turbulence itself, in five-dimensional phase space, one eddy at a time.

The ladder of description

To see why that calculation is so expensive — and why a surrogate is not a luxury but a necessity — you have to understand that a plasma can be described at several levels of detail, and that each level buys tractability by throwing away information. Fusion modeling is the art of choosing the coarsest description that still keeps the physics you need.

At the bottom of the ladder is the particle description: track every ion and electron through the electromagnetic fields, one Newtonian trajectory at a time. It is exact and it is hopeless — a cubic metre of fusion plasma holds far too many particles to follow individually, and no computer that will ever be built could carry them all. So you climb.

The next rung is the kinetic description. Instead of tracking individual particles, you track a distribution function — a smooth cloud in the six-dimensional space of position and velocity that says how many particles are, statistically, at each place moving at each speed. This is where the honest turbulence physics lives, and it is governed by a kinetic equation for how that cloud evolves. But six dimensions is a brutal price, so fusion physicists use a specialized simplification called gyrokinetics. The trick exploits a fact about magnetized plasma: each particle spirals tightly around a magnetic field line, thousands of times faster than anything interesting happens to its overall drift. You do not care about the fast spiral; you care about the guiding centre it spirals around. Gyrokinetics averages the spiral away, collapsing six dimensions to five and removing the fastest, least interesting timescale — and that single act of averaging is what makes first-principles turbulence simulation possible at all.

Climb once more and you reach the fluid description, which stops tracking the velocity cloud entirely and keeps only its bulk moments — density, flow, pressure — the way you describe water without tracking every molecule. Fluid models are fast and they are indispensable, but they need a closure: an assumption, imported from outside, about the quantities they threw away. And the most important closure of all is the turbulent heat flux — precisely the number gyrokinetics computes and fluid models cannot. At the top of the ladder sits magnetohydrodynamics, MHD, which treats the whole plasma as a single conducting fluid and is the right tool for large-scale stability but blind to the microscopic turbulence underneath.

Every rung of the ladder trades detail for speed, and the whole discipline is choosing the coarsest description that still tells the truth — and then paying, once, in gyrokinetic cycles, to compute the one closure the fast models cannot. The reason the confinement question is the most expensive in the program is now plain: it lives on the kinetic rung, in five dimensions, and it cannot be answered honestly from any rung above it. You either pay the gyrokinetic cost or you guess.

A zoo of instabilities, and how you name them

The turbulence that leaks heat out of a tokamak is not one thing. It is a whole zoo of microscopic instabilities, each with its own trigger, its own signature, and its own remedy, and a twin that hopes to predict confinement has to know which animals are in the cage.

The transport they drive is, by long convention, sorted into three kinds. Classical transport is the irreducible minimum: particles bump into each other and random-walk across the field. Neoclassical transport adds the corrections that come from the doughnut geometry itself — particles that get trapped in the weaker field on the outboard side trace fat "banana" orbits that let them wander farther. Both of these are calculable and, it turns out, small. What dominates real machines is the third kind, historically called anomalous transport precisely because for decades no one could explain why the heat leaked out so much faster than classical and neoclassical theory allowed. The answer, now settled, is turbulence — and the turbulence is driven by drift-wave instabilities feeding on the very gradients that make the plasma useful.

The main offenders have names worth knowing, because the twin has to resolve each one. The ion-temperature-gradient mode feeds on the steep ion temperature profile and is usually the dominant heat leak in the core. Its electron-scale cousin, the electron-temperature-gradient mode, does the same on a finer scale. The trapped-electron mode exploits those banana-orbit electrons. And the microtearing mode is a subtler, magnetic instability that tears and reconnects field lines on a tiny scale, channelling electron heat out through the plasma's edge. That edge is where the highest-stakes physics lives. A well-run tokamak spontaneously forms a pedestal — a narrow region at the boundary where the pressure gradient steepens dramatically and confinement jumps, the transition from ordinary low-confinement operation to the high-confinement mode that every reactor design quietly assumes. The pedestal is a gift and a hazard at once: it lifts performance, but it also stores energy that can be dumped in sudden bursts, the edge-localized modes that flick damaging heat pulses at the wall. Getting the pedestal right — steep enough to confine, controlled enough not to bite — is one of the hardest jobs the twin has.

How do you tell these instabilities apart in a real plasma, where they all contribute at once? You fingerprint them. Each mode has a characteristic frequency, a characteristic spatial scale, and a characteristic ratio between the fluctuations it produces in density and in magnetic field. Modern internal-fluctuation diagnostics can measure those signatures directly, and by comparing the measured fingerprint against what a gyrokinetic simulation predicts for each candidate mode, you can identify which instability is actually running the show in a given discharge. It is genuinely like forensic identification: not "the plasma is turbulent" but "this mode, at this location, is carrying this fraction of the heat."

That fingerprinting is also where fast, learned tools first entered fusion modeling, years before the surrogates of this program. Because a full gyrokinetic scan is far too slow to run inside an operating tokamak, physicists built reduced models — compact approximations, some of them frankly heuristic, that predict which modes will be unstable and how fast they will grow from a handful of local parameters, quickly enough to guide an experiment in progress. Neural networks trained on gyrokinetic databases pushed this further, delivering near-instant estimates of instability growth and even rapid reconstructions of the plasma equilibrium itself. Those early fast-surrogate successes are the direct ancestors of the transport surrogate at the heart of this chapter. The idea is the same one, grown up: pay the exact physics once, learn the shape of its answer, and thereafter reply in the blink of an eye.

Every design in this book rests on an assumption about how well its plasma holds heat. The twin exists to turn that assumption into a computed result.

That is the single most expensive question in the whole program, and until recently we answered it the way the field always has — with a reduced model, a fast approximation that captures the physics in broad strokes and runs in seconds. Reduced models are indispensable. They are also not proof. The point of the simulation program is to replace the assumption with a first-principles answer, validate that answer against reality, and then compress it into a tool fast enough to redesign the machine in an afternoon.

A machine that has to run in two places at once

Before the physics, a word about time. A fusion generator is a stack of coupled processes whose natural timescales span ten orders of magnitude — the cross-layer timing ladder laid out in full earlier in this chapter, from the microsecond events that can wreck the machine to the months of fuel logistics.

This is why the twin is not a single program. There is the design twin — slow, first-principles, exact, taking hours of supercomputer time to answer one question about one operating point — and there is the predictive shadow, the fast twin that runs alongside a live plasma, integrated fifty to a hundred milliseconds ahead of reality, catching trouble before it arrives. They are the same physics at opposite ends of the time ladder, and the bridge between them is the central trick of this chapter: the surrogate, a learned model that inherits the exact twin's accuracy and the shadow's speed. Get that bridge right and microsecond design exploration becomes possible — you can ask the machine ten thousand "what if" questions in the time it used to take to ask one.

The pipeline: an ordinary desktop, an extraordinary discipline

The exact turbulence physics runs in a first-principles nonlinear gyrokinetic code — the kind of tool that a decade ago lived only on national supercomputers. The program runs it two ways. On the ground is a single workstation, a 28-core machine with 768 gigabytes of memory, on which the full gyrokinetic suite is built, validated, and used for development. In the cloud are the accelerators — banks of high-end GPUs rented by the hour — where the heavy nonlinear runs actually execute. The workstation writes the problem; the cloud solves it; the answer comes home.

The unglamorous detail I want to dwell on is that this pipeline is bit-exact. A calculation launched from the desktop and run on a rented cloud GPU returns results identical, to the last bit, to the same calculation run locally. That sounds like a triviality. It is not. It is the entire reproducibility case in one property. If the cloud and the desktop disagreed even in the last decimal place, you could never be sure whether a result was physics or an artifact of where it happened to run — and a fusion design that cannot be independently rerun is not a design, it is an anecdote. Bit-exactness means anyone, anywhere, on any comparable hardware, can regenerate the numbers. It is the same philosophy that governs the published papers: every headline reproduces off a script from a single random seed. The twin holds itself to the standard we hold the physics to.

Validate against reality, then — and only then — trust the model

Here is the step that separates a twin from a mirror, and it is worth stating as a rule because the whole credibility of the program turns on it.

You never trust a simulation of your own machine until the same simulation, unchanged, has reproduced an experiment someone already ran on a real machine.

So before the code is ever pointed at Hyperion, it is pointed at a real tokamak discharge — a shot from an existing, operating device, with published measurements of how much heat actually leaked out of that real plasma. The code is given the real machine's geometry and profiles and asked, from first principles, to predict the measured heat flux. If it reproduces the experiment, within the error bars, without being tuned to do so, then and only then has it earned the right to be believed about a machine that does not yet exist. This is the difference between "our model says Hyperion works" and "our model reproduces reality, and our model says Hyperion works." The first is a claim. The second is evidence.

I put the validation step deliberately before the design study in the plan, not after, because the temptation runs the other way. It is tempting to simulate your own machine first, get an encouraging number, and validate later if time allows. That ordering quietly poisons everything downstream, because once you have seen the answer you want, every subsequent modeling choice is contaminated by it. Validate first, against a discharge you did not design and cannot fudge, and the design result that follows is honest by construction.

A validation shot, worked through

The rule above — never trust a simulation of your own machine until the same code, unchanged, has reproduced an experiment someone else already ran — is easy to state and laborious to honor. So let me walk one validation through, step by step, because the discipline lives in the details, not the slogan.

You begin by choosing a discharge from an existing, operating tokamak — a real "shot," fired years ago on a machine you had no hand in designing, with published, peer-reviewed measurements of two things: the plasma profiles inside that shot, and, crucially, how much heat actually leaked out of it. The fact that you did not design the machine is not incidental. It is the entire point. A shot you cannot influence is a shot you cannot flatter. It sits in the literature as a fixed fact, indifferent to what you wish your code would say.

Then you set the problem up honestly. You hand the gyrokinetic code that machine's real geometry and its measured profiles — the density and temperature and, above all, the gradients of those profiles at the radius you are testing, because it is the gradients that feed the turbulence. And then you do the hard thing: you tell the code nothing about the answer. You do not reveal the measured heat flux. You do not reach in and tune a coefficient to nudge the prediction toward the known result. The code integrates the turbulence from first principles — the ion-temperature-gradient mode and its cousins tearing the plasma into a froth of microscopic eddies — running forward until the transport saturates and the heat flux settles to a steady value. Hours of GPU time later, it reports a number it derived without ever being told what it was supposed to find.

Only now do you look. You set the computed heat flux beside the measured one. If they agree within the experiment's error bars — and agree without any tuning to make them — then the code has earned something it can earn no other way: the right to be believed about Hyperion, a machine that does not yet exist. This is the exact moment a claim turns into evidence. Before it, you have "our model says Hyperion confines heat well enough." After it, you have "our model reproduces a real plasma it was never shown, and that same model says Hyperion confines heat well enough." Only the second sentence can carry the weight of a design.

It is worth sitting with what a failure here would have meant, because that is what gives the passing grade its value. Suppose the computed flux had come out at half the measured value. You would not, in that case, have a Hyperion result you merely needed to caveat. You would have a modeling bug wearing the costume of a physics prediction — and every encouraging number the code later produced about your own machine would be worthless, because you would have no way to tell physics from artifact. That is precisely why the validation step is placed before the design study in the plan and never after: the ground has to be proven solid before you build on it, not once the building is up.

And validation is never one triumphant checkmark. The honest version reports the match together with its error bar, flags the radii where the agreement is tight and the ones where it frays, and treats near-marginal points — the delicate cases sitting right at the edge of stability — with extra suspicion, because a coarse calculation will cheerfully report a clean answer there that is simply wrong. A twin earns trust one validated shot at a time, and it keeps a ledger of exactly how far that trust extends.

Surrogates: turning a supercomputer into a pocket calculator

A first-principles turbulence run is accurate and slow. One saturated nonlinear calculation — the kind that tells you how much heat truly leaks out at one set of gradients, one safety factor, one value of plasma pressure — costs hours of GPU time. To map the whole operating space of a machine, you need hundreds of them. That is a database, and a database is exactly what a machine-learning model wants to eat.

A surrogate is a neural network trained on that database to reproduce the slow code's answer in a fraction of the time. Feed it the plasma conditions; it returns the heat flux — not by solving the physics, but by having learned the shape of the solution across every point it was trained on. The first-generation transport surrogate in the program was trained on a fast reduced (quasilinear) transport model rather than the full nonlinear code, as a proof of the mechanism, and it reached a coefficient of determination of R² = 0.999 against its training physics. The successor, now that the first-principles database is being generated, is trained on the exact nonlinear code itself — inheriting its accuracy instead of the reduced model's approximation. Same architecture, better teacher.

What that R² buys is worth translating carefully, because the number hides the point.

``` One first-principles turbulence calculation: ~hours on a cloud GPU One surrogate query for the same answer: ~microseconds on a laptop

Accuracy retained by the surrogate: R² = 0.999

```

In plain words: R² = 0.999 means the surrogate accounts for 99.9 percent of the variation in the exact code's answers — the two agree to about a part in a thousand across the operating space. And it delivers that agreement roughly a billion times faster. That ratio is not a convenience; it is a change in what design is. When one physics answer costs hours, you evaluate a handful of candidate machines and pick the least-bad. When one answer costs microseconds, you let an optimizer roam the entire design space — size, field, shape, gradients — evaluating millions of variants, and you find the operating point that is genuinely best rather than merely acceptable. The surrogate turns the most expensive question in fusion into something you can ask on a laptop between sips of coffee. That is how a design gets de-risked: not by trusting one calculation, but by exhausting the space around it.

A design search, worked through

Once the transport surrogate returns a heat flux in microseconds instead of hours, the design search itself — trading the field's old habit of stopping at the first acceptable machine for an optimizer that roams the whole space of candidate Hyperions and finds the genuinely best one — is the optimization story told in full earlier in this chapter. What matters for the twin is the shape it takes here: because Hyperion sits close to the ion-temperature-gradient threshold, the search does not hunt for a design that merely passes but for the operating point that sits deepest inside the feasible region — robust to exactly the gradient error bars a knife-edge design could not survive. That is what de-risking a design means in practice: not trusting one calculation, but exhausting the space around it so thoroughly that you know your chosen point is not a lucky accident.

The burner's twin, and a real net-gain result

The breeder is a tokamak, and its turbulence is a tokamak's turbulence. The burner is another creature altogether — a D–³He tandem mirror, a straight magnetic bottle some 440 metres long, stoppered at each end by colossal mirror coils reaching 26.49 tesla, burning a fuel so clean it sheds only about 5.4 percent of its energy as neutrons. Picture it: not a doughnut of fire chasing its own tail, but a river of plasma running the length of a city block, pinched at both ends by two of the most powerful magnetic corks ever conceived. A tandem mirror does not confine plasma by bending it into a ring; it confines it by squeezing it between those corks. Whether that works — whether the machine produces more power than it spends holding the plasma in — comes down to a delicate balance between the pressure in the central cell and the far higher pressure in the plugs.

The consequence for the twin is fundamental: a mirror is not a Grad–Shafranov machine, so almost none of the tokamak's equilibrium and turbulence machinery carries over. The confining physics is the force balance along the axis — how the pressure profile from the low-field central cell up to the towering plug field holds together — and the twin for the burner is built around that balance rather than around cross-field turbulent transport. Two machines, two twins, one discipline: build the exact model, validate it, compress it into a surrogate. The physics under the surrogate could hardly be more different; the method on top of it is identical.

We built a surrogate for that balance too, trained on the burner's mirror force-balance model. It reached R² = 0.98, and it returned a result I find genuinely encouraging: the machine crosses into net power gain when the plug-to-central-cell density ratio reaches about 13.8. The design target for that ratio is 16, comfortably above the crossover, at which point the engineering gain lands near Q_E ≈ 1.318 — more electricity out than in. That is exactly the kind of margin you want to see fall out of a surrogate: not a knife-edge, but a design point sitting on the safe side of the threshold with room to spare. It is a small, honest, computed result that says the burner's core premise holds.

The gaps, told plainly

I would not trust this chapter — you should not trust this chapter — if it were all clean R² values and comfortable margins. It is not. Three things in the program do not reconcile, and each teaches something.

The first linear map was noisy. The opening step of the turbulence campaign is a linear stability map: sweep the plasma gradients and find where the instabilities switch on and how fast they grow. Our first pass came out under-converged near the margin — the near-threshold modes, the ones sitting right at the edge of stability, were not integrated long enough or resolved finely enough to trust. Near-marginal modes are notoriously delicate; a coarse calculation will happily report a clean answer that is simply wrong. The fix is not clever, it is disciplined: longer integration, more radial resolution, rerun. That sweep is running as this is written. I mention it because a design program that never shows you a noisy first result is a program that is hiding its first results.

Hyperion sits close to the turbulence threshold. When we swept the gradients, the real machine came out weakly unstable to the ion-temperature-gradient mode near threshold — turbulent, but not violently so, right in the sensitive regime where small changes in the assumed gradients move the answer a lot. That is not a problem to paper over; it is a flag that says the operating point must be pinned down with the machine's real profile gradients, not the placeholder gradients used to explore the space. The geometry of Hyperion is locked and real. The gradients that ride on top of it are still being nailed to the design, and until they are, the confinement number carries an honest error bar.

And the one we abandoned. The burner needs a number called η_α — the efficiency with which the energy of fusion-born alpha particles is channelled back into the fuel ions rather than lost. We tried to compute it with a Fokker–Planck kinetic prototype, the natural tool for the job. It did not work.
