I will put no numbers of that kind in this book, because the honest ones do not exist yet.

The logistics are their own frontier. Even granting extraction, the fuel has to come home: collected, purified, and returned across roughly four hundred thousand kilometers to plants on Earth. The saving grace, again, is energy density — the annual payload is small — but "small and from the Moon" is still an unsolved supply chain, dependent on launch cadence and return capability that are being built for other purposes and on other timelines.

And it is outside our control. This is the part that separates this gate from every other gate in the book, and I want it to land with full force. The physics of the burner is ours; we solved it and published it and you can check our work. The lunar supply is not ours. It depends on programs, companies, and national ambitions we do not run and cannot command. We have stated it, in our own technical library, as exactly what it is: an external bet. The most we have done to hedge it is to make sure the expertise is in the room — the founding team deliberately includes a specialist in lunar helium-3 — but expertise on the team is not the same as fuel in the tank, and I will not dress it up as if it were.

None of this is a reason to look away. It is a reason to sequence the program so that nothing near-term depends on the bet paying off — to build a company that can survive being wrong about the Moon. The breeder is profitable on materials without ever setting foot on the lunar surface. The demonstrator and the first commercial burners run on bred and decayed helium-3 from Earth. The Moon is the gate on scale — on the fleet, not on survival. If lunar helium-3 arrives on schedule, the ceiling lifts and the sky, quite literally, is no longer the limit. If it is late, the program does not fall; it simply grows more slowly, on breeder-limited fuel, until the fuel landscape changes. That is what it means to build a company that can wait — and patience, in a field littered with the wreckage of the impatient, is its own kind of superpower.

The third forty, made physical

Now the pieces fit together, and the horizon stops being an abstraction and becomes a road you can walk with your finger on the map.

Follow the fuel through the plan. Around 2032, the first test burner — a 100-megawatt demonstrator — proves the physics on breeder-made helium-3. Around 2036, the first commercial units come online, roughly a gigawatt apiece, still fed from the limited terrestrial and bred supply, still counted in ones and twos because that is all the fuel allows. Then, around 2040, if the lunar economy delivers, the fuel constraint that has capped everything simply lifts — the ceiling dissolves. A fleet that was rationed to a handful of units by the scarcity of a single isotope can begin to grow the way infrastructure grows, the way railroads and grids and the internet grew: toward something like ninety units, ninety gigawatts, by 2050.

That last number is the third forty wearing work clothes. Q40 is the fortyfold physics of the reaction. Forty dollars a megawatt-hour is the price the burner can reach when its fuel is abundant and cheap rather than scarce and contested — and the single largest lever on that price is where the helium-3 comes from. And within forty years is the runway this whole staged march needs: breeders first, demonstrator next, a first commercial cohort after that, and only then — patiently, dependent on a frontier we do not own — a fleet fueled from the surface of another world. The horizon is not a slogan. It is the honest sum of how long each of these gates takes to open, added up without cheating.

I called this the most speculative chapter, and it is. But notice what kind of speculation it is, because the distinction is everything. Nothing here asks you to believe in undiscovered physics or a miracle machine that violates a law of nature. The reaction is real and its energy is settled at 18.35 MeV. The regolith holds the fuel; the Apollo samples proved it in a laboratory decades ago. The mechanism to release it is a hot plate, not an alchemist's dream. What is unproven is the engineering and the enterprise of doing it at scale, on time, and off the Earth — and unproven is a very different word from impossible. The first fusion company most people imagined would need one impossible thing to be true. This one needs a series of difficult things to be done, in order, by people who have said out loud, in print, which ones they cannot yet do.

The road that began with two machines, in the last chapter, ends here — with a fuel that was salted into the lunar soil by the Sun over billions of years, grain by grain, silent and waiting, it turns out, for a reason to be dug up. There is something almost mythic in it: the same star that lights our days seeding the Moon with the fuel to light our nights, and leaving it there across the whole span of life on Earth until a species clever enough to burn it finally arrived. Whether we reach it on the timeline I have drawn is the open question of this book. That we should try, and that the physics rewards us if we succeed, is not.

The Road to $40 a Megawatt-Hour, Worked

Everything in this chapter has been building to a single number, and it is time to show the arithmetic behind it. Not the company's private ledgers — those stay private, and I will say plainly where the line is — but the structure of the number: the equation every power plant on Earth is judged by, and the specific physical levers by which this machine is engineered to drive that equation down to forty dollars a megawatt-hour. You do not have to take the number on faith. You have to see how it is built.

The one equation that decides everything

The price of electricity from any plant is captured by a single ratio the whole industry uses — the levelized cost of energy, or LCOE. Stripped to its bones it is this:

**LCOE = ( CRF · Capital + Fixed O&M + Fuel ) ÷ ( 8,760 · Power · Capacity Factor )**

Read it slowly, because the whole strategy of this book lives inside it. The top is what the plant costs to build and run each year: the capital cost spread out over the plant's life by a capital-recovery factor (CRF), plus the annual cost of operating it, plus the annual cost of its fuel. The bottom is how many megawatt-hours it actually sells in a year: the number of hours in a year (8,760), times the plant's power rating, times the fraction of the time it is actually running — its capacity factor.

To make the electron cheap, you make the top small and the bottom large. That is the entire game. And a fusion machine has four levers on that ratio that no fossil or fission plant can pull the same way.

The price of power is one ratio: what it costs to build and feed, over how much it actually makes. Every design choice in this book is a move on that ratio.

Lever one — direct conversion attacks the bottom of the ratio

Every thermal power plant on Earth — coal, gas, fission, and most fusion concepts — makes electricity the same way James-Watt-era way: heat water, spin a turbine, and surrender more than half the energy to the laws of thermodynamics as waste heat. That Carnot penalty is a tax on the bottom of the LCOE ratio: you paid to make the energy, then you throw most of it away before it reaches the wire.

The burner refuses that tax. Because its D–³He reaction releases its energy as charged particles rather than neutrons — a neutron fraction of just 5.44 percent — most of that energy can be caught and turned to electricity directly, decelerated against a voltage instead of boiled into steam. The worked power balance in this chapter lands the engineering gain at Q_E ≈ 1.318, with direct conversion recovering hundreds of megawatts that a steam cycle would have thrown away. More electricity out of the same reaction means more megawatt-hours on the bottom of the ratio — and every megawatt-hour added there pushes the price down.

Lever two — firm power fills the hours

Look again at the bottom of the equation: capacity factor, the fraction of the year the plant actually runs. This is where intermittent sources bleed. A solar farm's capacity factor sits near a quarter; a wind farm's near a third. They are cheap to build and then idle most of the time, which quietly triples or quadruples the price of every hour they do deliver, because the capital is spread over far fewer megawatt-hours.

Fusion is firm: it runs day and night, in any weather, on demand. A fusion plant is engineered for the capacity factors of baseload infrastructure — the high-eighties to mid-nineties percent — the same league as the best fission plants. That is not a small edit to the LCOE; it is a doubling or tripling of the denominator against an intermittent competitor. Firmness is not just a grid-reliability virtue. It is one of the largest single levers on the price.

Lever three — the fuel term, and why it runs through the Moon

Here is the lever that decides whether the whole thing works, and the one I will be most honest about. The fuel term sits on top of the ratio, and for the burner it is dominated by the cost of helium-3.

On Earth, helium-3 is so scarce that the fuel alone would swamp any plausible power price — the burner, run on terrestrial helium-3, simply loses. That is not a number I am hiding; it is a physical fact about a substance that barely exists on this planet. The fuel term only becomes small when helium-3 becomes abundant and cheap, and the only place we know of that holds it in quantity is the lunar regolith. This is why the road to forty dollars runs, improbably, through the Moon — and why I place the $40/MWh milestone after the lunar-helium-3 gate around 2040, not before. Before that gate, the fuel term dominates and the price is high; after it, the fuel term collapses and the target comes into reach. The sensitivity of the whole LCOE to this one input is the honest heart of the economics.

Lever four — the learning curve attacks the capital term

The last lever is the capital term, and it falls the oldest way in industry: by building the same machine more than once. The first-of-a-kind unit pays for every mistake exactly once — the drawings, the jigs, the untrained crews, the first regulatory license. The second unit inherits all of it. Build times fall down the curve — for the burners, roughly three years to two and a half to two — and every repetition drives the capital term of the ratio down. A single heroic reactor never gets cheap. A fleet does. The commercial units are deliberately sized at about a gigawatt each precisely so they can be financed, sited, and repeated fast enough to ride that curve.

The arithmetic, worked — with public numbers only

I promised to show the work, so here it is, done the only honest way a public book can do it: with ratios and published reference values, never with the company's private inputs. You do not need our capital cost to see how the number is reached. You need a starting point anyone can look up, and then the four levers, each expressed as a factor that multiplies the price up or down. Follow the chain and the forty-dollar figure stops being a claim and becomes a consequence.

Start where the whole industry starts: the capital-recovery factor. Spread a plant's build cost over a thirty-year life at a discount rate around seven percent and the standard formula — CRF = r(1+r)ⁿ ⁄ ((1+r)ⁿ − 1) — returns about 0.081 per year. That is not a Kronos number; it is the arithmetic every utility on Earth runs, and it means roughly eight cents of annualized cost for every dollar of capital, before a single electron is sold. Every lever below is a fight against that eight cents.

Now the bridge. Independent, widely published estimates put the levelized cost of the incumbents in these bands — and I use their numbers, not mine, precisely so you can check them:

SourcePublished LCOE band (USD/MWh)Firm & clean?
Utility-scale solar (no storage)~30–90Clean, not firm
Onshore wind~30–75Clean, not firm
Solar + multi-hour storage~60–210Clean, partly firm
Combined-cycle gas~45–110Firm, not clean
New-build fission~140–220Firm & clean
Burner target (this book)~40Firm & clean

Read that table honestly and the burner's ambition is plain: land in the cheap rows — down where unfirmed solar and wind sit, at roughly thirty to ninety dollars a megawatt-hour — while keeping the firm-and-clean column, a combination no existing row holds at once. Here is the multiplicative path there, each factor a lever from the pages above, applied to a first-of-a-kind fusion price that would otherwise start in fission's neighborhood, north of $150 a megawatt-hour:

  • Direct conversion removes the thermal tax. A steam-cycle fusion plant throws away more than half its energy; the burner's charged-particle conversion keeps far more of it on the wire. More saleable megawatt-hours from the same reaction pulls the price down by roughly a third — call it a ×0.65.
  • Firmness protects the denominator. Run at a baseload capacity factor near ninety percent instead of an intermittent quarter-to-third, and the capital spreads over three to four times the megawatt-hours. Against an intermittent competitor that is a ×0.4–0.5; against an already-firm one it simply keeps the denominator from collapsing.
  • The learning curve grinds the capital term. First-of-a-kind pays for every mistake once; by the tenth gigawatt-class unit, published learning rates for manufactured energy hardware (roughly 10–20 percent cost reduction per doubling of units) compound to a ×0.4–0.6 on the capital-driven part of the price. A fleet is cheap in a way a single heroic reactor never is.
  • Cheap lunar helium-3 collapses the fuel term. On terrestrial helium-3 the fuel line alone would dwarf every other term and the exercise fails; with lunar supply after ~2040 the fuel term falls back into the rounding — a ×1 instead of a ×(many).

Chain the middle three against a first-of-a-kind starting price and the destination is not mysterious: 150-plus, times roughly 0.65, times roughly 0.5, times roughly 0.5, lands in the low tens of dollars per megawatt-hour — with the fuel term held down by the Moon rather than allowed to explode. That is the arithmetic of forty dollars. Not a spreadsheet I am asking you to trust; a published starting point and four factors you can argue with one at a time.

And here is the sensitivity ranking, because the four levers are not equal. The one that can kill the number outright is the fuel term — miss cheap helium-3 and nothing else saves it; it is a switch, not a dial. The one that does the most continuous work is the learning curve, because it compounds over a fleet and never stops. Firmness decides whether you are even in the right comparison — it is what lets the burner be judged against gas and fission rather than against unfirmed solar. And direct conversion is the enabling multiplier that makes the machine worth building at all, though its marginal effect on the final price is the smallest of the four. Ranked by fragility: fuel first, learning curve second, firmness third, direct conversion fourth. That ordering is the risk profile of the forty-dollar electron.

Putting it together — and where the private line is

Pull the four levers at once and the path to forty dollars is legible: direct conversion and firm operation multiply the megawatt-hours on the bottom; the learning curve grinds the capital term down; and cheap lunar helium-3 collapses the fuel term that would otherwise dominate. Under those conditions — a mature, repeated, gigawatt-class burner fleet running on lunar fuel — the arithmetic lands near the forty-dollar target. Miss any one lever and it does not: skip direct conversion and the thermal tax returns; run intermittently and the denominator shrinks; stall the fleet and the capital never amortizes; and without cheap helium-3 the fuel term alone sinks it.

Now the line I promised. I have shown you the equation, the levers, and the direction each one pushes — the work. What I have deliberately not printed are the specific dollar inputs: the capital cost of a unit, the price of a kilogram of lunar helium-3, the operating budget, the margins. Those are real numbers the company holds with its partners, and a public book is the wrong place for them; their absence changes none of the physics you have just seen. The forty-dollar figure is not a spreadsheet I am asking you to trust. It is the target the entire engineering program — the low-neutron fuel, the direct converter, the firm duty cycle, the fleet, the lunar supply chain — was built to reach, and every lever above is a checkable, physical reason it is reachable rather than wishful.

I will show you the equation and the levers. The private dollars stay private — and they have to, because the honesty of this book depends on never dressing a business projection up as a law of physics.

That is the road to forty dollars: not a promise, but a ratio, and four physical hands on it.

Safe by Design: Waste, Risk, and the Environmental Case

There are two questions worth asking of any machine that makes energy, and most of the argument about nuclear power for the last seventy years has quietly confused them — to everyone's cost. The first is: what does it do when everything works? The second, the one that actually keeps people awake at three in the morning, is: what does it do when everything goes wrong? A coal plant working perfectly is a slow catastrophe, filling the sky with the carbon of buried forests; a coal plant failing is mostly a local one. Fission inverts that — usually benign, rarely terrible. The great inversion of fusion — the thing that took me years to state plainly enough to trust — is that it is safe in both registers at once. When it works, its waste stream is modest and finite. When it fails, it simply stops. Neither claim is a slogan, and I will not let you take either on faith. Each falls out of the physics itself, and each comes with an honest cost that I intend to put on the table in front of you rather than under it.

The reactor that wants to stop

Start with failure, because that is where the fear lives, and fear deserves a straight answer.

The deepest safety fact about fusion is structural, woven into the concept, and it is the exact opposite of the fact that governs a fission reactor. A fission reactor runs on a chain reaction: each splitting nucleus throws off neutrons that split more nuclei, which throw off more neutrons still, and the entire engineering art is holding that self-amplifying avalanche at precisely the knife-edge of "just barely self-sustaining." The fuel is arranged so that the reaction wants to continue — it is loaded with years of energy at once, a coiled spring — and the control systems exist to restrain something that, left alone, runs away from you. Even after the chain reaction is stopped, the fuel keeps generating heat from its own radioactive decay for days, and that residual heat must be actively carried away or the core cooks itself. The failures that live in public memory are, at bottom, failures to remove that decay heat. The hazard is inherent in the concept: a large inventory of energy that stays hot on its own, whether you want it to or not.

Fusion has no chain reaction. None. There is no neutron multiplication holding the process together, no critical mass, no configuration anywhere in the machine that amplifies itself. A fusion plasma is the single hardest thing in the known universe to keep going — that is the entire difficulty of the field, the reason it took seventy years and the labor of thousands — and that same difficulty is, read from the other side, the whole of its passive safety. The plasma has to be driven every instant: heated to a hundred million degrees, hotter than the core of the Sun, held in shape by fields, fed fuel a fraction of a gram at a time. Interrupt any of it — cut the heating, drop a magnet, lose the fuel feed, spring a leak — and the reaction does not surge. It quenches. In under a second the plasma cools below the threshold where fusion can occur, and it is simply over. You do not have to do anything to stop it. Stopping is its natural state; running is the achievement you fight for every microsecond.

A fusion plasma is the hardest thing on Earth to keep going. That is precisely why it is safe: the reaction you must fight to sustain is a reaction that cannot run away.

The second structural fact is inventory, and it is just as reassuring. At any instant, the amount of fusion fuel actually inside the burning chamber is on the order of grams — seconds of operation, no more. A fission core holds years of fuel; a fusion chamber holds a single breath of it, replenished continuously like a flame fed a whisker of gas at a time. There is simply no large store of energy sitting in the reaction volume waiting to be released by an accident. Whatever can go wrong can only reach the fuel that happens to be in flight, and that fuel, denied its heating and its magnetic cage, is inert within moments. The catastrophic accident that fission engineering spends its whole discipline preventing does not have a mechanism to occur here. This is not because we have engineered a cleverer safety system than anyone before us. It is because the concept never offered the failure mode in the first place — the door was never built into the wall.

I want to be careful, because "inherently safe" is a phrase the field has abused, and I have no wish to add to the abuse. Fusion is not hazard-free. It concentrates energy, it uses cryogenics and high magnetic fields and, in the breeder, a radioactive gas; those are real industrial hazards demanding serious engineering, and a magnet failure or a plasma disruption can wreck expensive hardware in an instant. On disruptions the design carries its own numbers rather than a hope: the current quench completes in 7–19 milliseconds, halo currents load the vessel at up to 35 percent of the plasma current, and the runaway-electron avalanche at these parameters is severe — which is why shattered-pellet injection is carried as a hard design requirement, not an option (gate BR-L2-A10). What fusion does not have is the specific, terrifying failure mode of fission — the self-heating core that must be cooled or else. The correct claim is narrow and it is true: there is no meltdown here, because there is nothing that stays hot on its own, and there is no runaway, because there is no chain reaction to run away. That is the whole of it, and it is enough.

The honest neutron problem

Now the cost, stated as plainly as I know how, because this is exactly the place where fusion's advocates tend to go quiet and hope you do not notice. I would rather you noticed.

Fusion is clean at the fuel — but the deuterium–tritium reaction that the breeder runs on is not clean at the wall. When deuterium fuses with tritium, roughly four-fifths of the energy leaves as a neutron carrying 14 million electron-volts, and a neutron that energetic does not care about magnetic fields — it is electrically neutral, a ghost that walks straight through the cage. It flies straight out of the plasma and buries itself in whatever surrounds it — and in doing so it transmutes the surrounding atoms, knocking them into radioactive isotopes. This is activation, and it is the honest waste story of D–T fusion, the asterisk on the dream. The breeder, Hyperion, produces about 85.04 megawatts of fusion power, of which some 70.9 megawatts streams out as fast neutrons. It makes those neutrons deliberately — they are its product, the very tools that breed its tritium and qualify its materials — and there is no version of the machine that makes them without also activating its own structure. You cannot have the foundry without the fire, and the fire leaves marks.

So the breeder needs shielding, and it needs it in earnest: a thick neutron shield around the core, a tungsten-based jacket, roughly thirty centimetres of passive material standing between the neutron source and the outside world like a castle wall. And it needs a discipline the 2024 version of this book skated past — scheduled component replacement. The slender high-field centrepost that threads the machine sits directly in the neutron blast and cannot survive it indefinitely; it is designed as a consumable, replaced on the order of every one to two full-power-years, the way a furnace liner or a set of brake pads is replaced. The first wall and blanket components live under the same flux and are likewise finite-life parts. These are not failures. They are the running maintenance of a machine that makes neutrons for a living, and treating them as scheduled expenses we understand — rather than miracles of permanence we are still waiting for — is what lets the design be honest and buildable at once. But it means the breeder produces a stream of activated hardware over its life, and I will not pretend it doesn't.

The saving grace, and it is a large one, is what kind of radioactivity this is — a point I will come back to when we talk about waste, and it changes the whole complexion of the problem. But the near-term honesty is simple: the D–T breeder is a neutron machine, activation comes with it, and it is managed the industrial way, with shielding and with parts you plan to replace. Anyone who tells you a deuterium–tritium machine is clean at the wall is selling you the fuel and hiding the neutron behind their back.

The burner's cleaner ledger

Here the architecture of two machines earns its keep, because the machine that actually makes power for the grid is a fundamentally cleaner one — and the cleanliness is chosen, not wished for.

The burner does not run on deuterium–tritium. It runs on deuterium and helium-3, and that changes the neutron problem at its root rather than merely shielding against the symptom. The dominant D–³He reaction produces no neutron at all — it yields a proton and a helium nucleus, both charged, both steerable by magnetic fields, both catchable. Neutrons appear only as a side reaction, when two deuterium nuclei happen to fuse, and the burner is designed to hold that fraction low. At its design point the neutron power fraction is f_n ≈ 5.44% — low-neutron, and I am careful to say low-neutron and never aneutronic, because it is not zero and honesty forbids the rounder, prettier word. But set 5.44% against the breeder's roughly 80% and the difference is not incremental; it is categorical, a change of kind rather than degree. The burner is more than an order of magnitude cleaner at the wall than the D–T machine, purely by the choice of fuel.

That single number cascades through the whole design like a stone dropped in still water. Because the burner makes so few neutrons, it does not need a breeding blanket or a metre of shielding — a thin, low-activation shield suffices, a tungsten-based jacket doing structural and shielding duty at once. And because the charged fusion products carry their energy as motion rather than heat, the burner can convert them to electricity directly — steering the charged exhaust into a direct-energy-conversion train rather than boiling water to spin a turbine, capturing the energy in the coin it arrives in. No steam cycle. That is an environmental fact as much as an efficiency one: no enormous thermal-water demand, no waste-heat plume of the scale a steam plant throws off, a smaller and simpler plant to site near the data centres and installations it is meant to feed.

The breeder makes neutrons on purpose and shields against them honestly. The burner refuses to make them in the first place. That is why the fleet that powers the grid is the clean one.

I hold one line of candour here too, because low-neutron is not no-neutron, and the residual flux still matters. It sets the replacement lifetime of the high-field magnets at the plugs, and it still activates the structural shield, if far more slowly and far more shallowly than in the breeder. The burner is clean; it is not magic, and I would distrust anyone who told you it was. But the strategic point is real and it is the reason the company runs two machines instead of one: the dirty, neutron-rich work of making fuel is confined to a few breeders built and shielded for exactly that job, while the many machines that actually deliver firm power to the world run on the clean reaction. We did not stumble into that division by luck. We designed the neutrons into the foundry and out of the fleet, on purpose, from the first drawing.

Tritium, and why we breed it where we burn it

Tritium deserves its own reckoning, because it is the one genuinely radioactive material the breeder handles in quantity, and because handling it well is a safety decision, not just a plumbing one.

Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen with a half-life of about 12.3 years. Its radiation is weak — a low-energy beta that will not even penetrate skin — so the hazard is not external; you could hold a sealed source of it in your hand. The hazard is that it is hydrogen: it slips through materials like a rumour, it wants to become water, and if inhaled or ingested it can deliver a dose from the inside, where the body has no defence. It must therefore be contained with real rigour — multiple barriers, careful accounting, low working inventories. This is well-trodden ground; tritium has been handled at scale in civil and defence programmes for decades, and the practices are mature, not experimental.

The design decision that most improves the safety of the whole system is where the tritium lives. The breeder makes its own — that is the entire point of the lithium blanket, which catches the neutrons and breeds fresh tritium in place, at a tritium breeding ratio above one. Breeding on-site, above self-sufficiency, means the machine never has to have tritium delivered. And that quietly removes an entire category of risk that has haunted every fusion fuel-cycle proposal. Shipping tritium is the part of the fuel cycle where material is most exposed — in transit, across jurisdictions, in packages that can be lost, stolen, or diverted. A machine that grows its fuel where it burns it eliminates the tritium convoy altogether. On-site breeding with a ratio above one is not only how the physics closes; it is the safer and more secure architecture, because the safest gram of tritium is the one that is never on a truck, never on a manifest, never anywhere but inside the machine that made it.

The inventories, too, are deliberately small, and this is where the design's discipline shows most clearly. Older proposals for fusion breeders foundered precisely on tritium inventory — one classic concept would have needed something like 1.8 tonnes of it on hand, an amount its own authors admitted would be nearly impossible to license, a non-starter dressed as a design. Hyperion is sized so that its equilibrium tritium inventory sits around 6.2 kilograms, with startup holdings in the range of a dozen to a couple of dozen kilograms — an inventory that fits inside existing civil licensing precedent, roughly fifty times smaller than the concept that could not be licensed. The physics never forbade a small breeder; it forbade a large one. By sizing the machine to a real national requirement rather than to a maximised output, the inventory stays inside the envelope regulators already know how to license, and the hazard scales down with it. Modesty of ambition, here, is a safety feature.

Waste that has an end date

Now to the claim that matters most to anyone who has followed the politics of nuclear power for the last half-century — the argument that has stalled more reactors than any accident ever did: the waste.

Fusion produces no spent fuel. Let me be precise about what that sentence means, because it is the crux of the entire environmental case. Fission splits heavy atoms, and in doing so it manufactures two things that have to be isolated from the living world for a very long time: fission products, and — more stubbornly — transuranic elements like plutonium, forged when uranium absorbs neutrons without splitting. These long-lived actinides are why fission's high-level waste has to be sequestered for timescales measured in tens of thousands of years — longer than human writing has existed, out at the ragged edge of what any human institution can even promise to remember. Fusion makes none of them. There is no uranium in the machine, no plutonium made, no actinides, no spent-fuel assemblies, no self-heating waste that must be cooled in a pool for years before it can even be moved. That entire category — the one that has stalled fission politically for two generations and buried it under mountains and referendums — does not exist here.

What fusion does leave behind is the activated structure I was candid about earlier: the breeder's replaced centrepost, its spent blanket components, its inner wall — hardware made radioactive by the neutrons that passed through it. This is real waste and it must be managed; I will not wave it away. But it is a categorically gentler problem, for one reason that changes everything: it is a matter of materials choice, not of the fuel. The radioactivity is in the steel and the tungsten and the ceramics, isotopes created by neutron capture, and the great majority of them are short- to medium-lived. Choose the structural materials well — the low-activation alloys the field has spent decades developing precisely for this moment — and the activated hardware decays not over ten thousand years but over decades to a century or two, after which much of it can be cleared or recycled back into new components rather than buried. Fusion's waste has an end date within the horizon of the institutions that will manage it — within the memory of a family, not a geology. That is the difference that matters, and it is not a small one.

The two waste questions, side by side.

>

How long? Fission's high-level waste must be isolated for tens of thousands of years, because it contains long-lived actinides like plutonium. Fusion makes no actinides; its waste is activated structure whose radioactivity decays over decades to a century or two.

>

How much, and what kind? Fusion produces no spent fuel and no self-heating high-level waste. It produces radioactive hardware — a maintenance stream, largely recyclable with low-activation materials — not a geological legacy.

>

The honest asterisk: the D–T breeder is the machine that generates most of this activated hardware; the low-neutron D–³He burner generates far less. The waste, like the neutrons, is concentrated in the foundry.

The helium-3 the breeder co-produces closes this loop in a small and genuinely beautiful way. Some of the surplus tritium is not delivered as fuel at all; it is simply set aside to decay, and what it decays into is helium-3 — a stable, valuable, entirely non-radioactive commodity, one of the scarcest useful isotopes on Earth. A fraction of the machine's radioactive inventory, left alone to age, ripens into a product worth more than gold by weight. It is the opposite of a waste stream: radioactive patience turned into strategic material, time itself doing the refining.

The security ledger

There is a dimension of nuclear safety that the public rarely separates from reactor accidents but that governments never stop thinking about, not for a single day: proliferation. A fission reactor is entangled, at the level of physics itself, with the making of weapons. It runs on enriched uranium — and the enrichment technology that makes reactor fuel is the same technology that, pushed a little further, makes weapons-grade material. It breeds plutonium in its core as an unavoidable consequence of splitting uranium, and plutonium is a weapons material. This is why civil fission programmes come wrapped in a global apparatus of safeguards, inspections, and treaties: the fuel cycle itself is dual-use down to its atoms. The peaceful reactor and the bomb are cousins who share a childhood.

Fusion severs most of that entanglement, and it is worth being precise about how, because precision is what separates a real claim from a comforting one. There is no uranium in either machine, no enrichment cascade, no plutonium bred, no fissile material produced or handled anywhere in the fuel cycle. The fuels are deuterium, drawn from seawater; lithium, to breed tritium; and helium-3. None of them is a weapons material, and none of the machine's products is a path to one. That removes the largest proliferation concern of the entire nuclear age at a single stroke.

I will not claim fusion is proliferation-proof, because honesty is the method of this book and the careful answer is more interesting than the triumphant one. Two residual concerns are worth naming. The first is tritium, which is a component of certain advanced weapons; the breeder makes and holds tritium, and that is exactly why it must be subject to rigorous accounting and control — the same mature safeguards that already govern tritium in civil and defence programmes worldwide. The second, more subtle, is that any intense neutron source could in principle be misused to irradiate materials for illicit purposes, which is a reason such machines belong inside a safeguards regime rather than outside one. But sit these against the fission ledger and the difference is stark: no enrichment, no plutonium, no fissile stockpile, no spent fuel from which weapons material could be separated. The neutrons are concentrated in a few breeders that can be watched closely, counted, and inspected; the many burners that make the power for the world handle no weapons-relevant material at all. Fusion does not abolish the need for nuclear security. It shrinks it to a small, well-understood, and geographically concentrated problem — which, in the world we actually live in, is an enormous improvement, perhaps the largest single gift the technology offers a nervous century.

Decommissioning, and the second life of the steel

Every power plant eventually reaches the end of its life, and how it dies is part of its environmental honesty — the final entry in the ledger, the one that is easy to leave off the brochure. Here fusion's advantage over fission is not rhetorical; it follows directly from the waste physics I laid out above, like a theorem from its axioms.

When a fission plant is retired, the operator faces spent fuel that must be guarded for millennia and a reactor structure contaminated in ways that make dismantling it a decades-long, hazardous, hugely expensive undertaking — a plant can take longer to take apart than it took to build and run. When a fusion plant is retired, there is no spent fuel to guard at all, and the radioactivity in the structure is activation — created by neutron capture in the steel, tungsten, and ceramics, and, if the materials were chosen well, dominated by short- to medium-lived isotopes. That single difference reshapes the whole end-of-life picture from a burden passed to the unborn into a job a maintenance crew can finish.

The concept that makes it work is low-activation materials, and the field has spent decades quietly developing them for exactly this moment, long before there was a machine to put them in. The idea is to build the neutron-facing structure out of elements that, when they capture a neutron, become isotopes that decay quickly rather than lingering for geological time — reduced-activation steels, silicon carbide composites, vanadium alloys, engineered so that after the machine is switched off its radioactivity falls steeply, like a fever breaking. Choose the alloys carelessly and you inherit a long-lived problem you did not have to create; choose them well, and the activated hardware decays over decades to a century or two, after which much of it can be cleared, or — better — recycled back into new components rather than buried.

That recycling is the part I find genuinely satisfying, almost poetic, and it is why I resist calling fusion's activated hardware "waste" without qualification. A retired centrepost or blanket module is not spent fuel with nowhere to go; it is expensive, high-performance metal that, after a decay period inside the reach of a human institution, can be remelted and rolled back into service — reincarnated as the heart of the next machine. The breeder's neutron-facing parts are already treated as scheduled consumables, replaced on the order of every one to two full-power-years — so the plant is, in effect, practising its own recycling loop throughout its operating life, not just at the end. The waste stream is a maintenance stream, and a maintenance stream of recyclable metal is a categorically gentler legacy than a geological repository that must outlast the civilisation that dug it. I keep the honest asterisk one more time: this depends on making the right materials choices up front, and on the recycling infrastructure existing to close the loop. Neither is automatic, and neither is free. But both are engineering and policy problems with end dates, not the open-ended custodianship — the promise made to people ten thousand years from now who cannot hold us to it — that fission's waste demands.

The life-cycle case

Zoom out from the machine to its whole footprint, because a fair environmental accounting has to include the steel and the concrete and the mining, not just the smokestack that isn't there. It is easy to look clean when you only count what leaves the chimney; the honest tally counts everything.

In operation, both machines emit no carbon dioxide, no sulphur, no particulates, no combustion products of any kind. There is nothing burning — that is the plain and radical fact at the center of it. The fuels are drawn from water and from lithium — deuterium is a stable, non-radioactive isotope present in every litre of seawater, and lithium is abundant — and a single day's fuel for a power plant is a quantity you could carry in your hands and hardly notice the weight. There is no fuel supply chain of the fossil scale: no continuous stream of tankers and trains and pipelines feeding a furnace that must be fed forever and refed tomorrow. The land footprint is small, the plant is firm — it runs day and night, weather notwithstanding, season notwithstanding — and the burner in particular, converting charged particles directly to electricity without a steam cycle, sidesteps the enormous cooling-water demand that every thermal plant, fossil or fission, carries as a hidden environmental cost.

Where fusion does spend its environmental budget is up front, in construction: in the steel and concrete of the plant, in the manufacture of high-temperature superconductor, in the mining and refining behind all of it. This is honest, and it is the same up-front carbon debt that wind, solar, and fission all carry — the emissions of building the thing, paid once, then amortised across decades of carbon-free generation. On a life-cycle basis that debt is small, of the order of other low-carbon sources and a world away from fossil generation, which pays not only to build but to burn, forever, with every hour of operation. Against fossil fuels the comparison is not close on any axis — carbon, air quality, water, land, or waste. Against fission, fusion trades away the two liabilities that have defined the older technology's public life — the runaway accident and the ten-thousand-year waste — and keeps the one virtue they share, which is a torrent of firm, dense, carbon-free power drawn from a vanishingly small amount of fuel.

The honest gates

I will end where I always try to, with what is not yet proven, because the safety case is only as good as its candour about the gates, and a safety argument that hides its own limits is the least safe thing of all.

No hardware has been built yet. The safety arguments in this chapter are structural — they follow from the physics of a driven plasma, from the neutron fractions of two well-characterised reactions, from the decay physics of activation products and the sizing of a tritium inventory. They are, I believe, sound, and I have shown you the numbers so you can judge for yourself rather than take my word. But demonstrated safety, the kind a regulator signs and an operator lives inside every day, comes with the first machine's operation, around 2030, not before, and not from any book. Construction of the first breeder begins in 2027; the safety case gets tested in steel and plasma after that, not in these pages.

And the specific costs stand, unhidden, in the daylight. The D–T breeder makes activation and needs real shielding and scheduled replacement of neutron-facing parts — say it plainly, always, every time. Tritium is a radioactive gas that demands rigorous containment, even if a small and well-precedented one. The burner is low-neutron, not no-neutron, and its residual flux still sets magnet lifetimes. None of these is a reason not to build. Each is a reason to build honestly — with the shielding drawn, the replacement parts scheduled, the inventory sized to precedent, and the minus signs printed right alongside the plus signs.

That is the environmental case, whole and without a thumb on the scale. A machine that stops the instant you stop driving it, because it never had a chain reaction to sustain. A fuel cycle that grows its own fuel on-site rather than shipping the dangerous part across the world on a truck. A waste stream with no spent fuel, no actinides, and an end date inside the reach of the institutions that will manage it — concentrated, honestly, in the few breeders that make the neutrons, and largely absent from the many burners that make the power. And a footprint that, measured across its whole life, sits among the cleanest sources we have and far below the ones we are straining to leave behind. Fusion is not perfectly clean, and I will never tell you it is. It is honestly clean — which, in the energy business, where every source has spent a century flattering itself, is the rarer and the more durable thing.

The Field, Honestly: Where This Approach Fits

I want to spend a chapter doing something that hype rarely lets a founder do: describe the rest of the field fairly, generously, without a single knife hidden behind my back, and then place my own work inside it without flattering myself. Fusion is not a race with one lane and one winner. It is a wide, crowded plain with several roads across it, and every road is being walked by serious, brilliant people who have given whole careers — sometimes whole lives — to the same star we are all chasing, the star we are all trying to bottle. Some of those roads will arrive. Some will not. I do not know for certain which is which, and I promise you that neither does anyone who tells you otherwise with a straight face. What I can do is draw the map honestly — by approach, not by any name — and then show you where our two-machine, materials-first design sits on it, what it borrows from the others, where it diverges, and what it is quietly betting that the rest are not.

This is the chapter where I am most tempted to be triumphant, and most determined not to be. The honest posture is not a decoration on the argument; it is the argument. If our approach is right, it will be right on the merits, and the merits do not need me to disparage anyone else's decades of work. A design that can only look good by making its neighbours look bad is a design I would not trust with a flashlight, let alone a star.

The families of effort

There are, broadly, four families of fusion effort in the world today. They differ in the shape of the machine, the fuel they burn, and the physics they are betting their futures on. Each has genuine strengths, real and hard-won. Each has a genuine problem it has not solved. Let me take them one at a time, and try to be as fair to each as I would want someone to be to me at my most vulnerable.

The great public tokamaks

The first family is the oldest and the largest: the giant, publicly funded, internationally shared tokamaks. These are the cathedral projects of fusion — enormous doughnut-shaped machines, built over decades, funded across borders and across political generations, designed to hold a ring of superheated plasma inside a cage of magnetic fields and burn the easiest fuel we have, deuterium and tritium. Like the medieval cathedrals, they are begun by people who will not live to see them finished, and that is not a flaw in them but a kind of nobility.

Their strength is real and should never be dismissed by anyone who understands what they cost to build. Nearly everything the entire field knows about confining a plasma at reactor conditions, we know because these machines taught us, degree by hard-won degree. They are where the physics of the burning plasma is being nailed down at full scale, with instrumentation and rigor that no small effort can match. When they achieve a milestone, it is a milestone for all of us, because it is measured under conditions closest to a real power reactor. If you want to know whether a plasma will behave the way theory says at the size and temperature of a true burner, these are the machines that answer the question. That is a public good of the highest order, and I am a grateful beneficiary of it — we all are, whether we admit it or not.

Their weakness is equally real, and it is not a physics weakness — it is a weakness of scale, time, and cost. These machines are vast because the conventional-tokamak recipe asks for size: to reach net gain with ordinary magnets and ordinary geometry, you build big, and big is slow and expensive and measured in decades. The timelines stretch across generations of scientists, careers begun and ended inside a single project. And because they burn deuterium and tritium, they inherit the neutron problem in full — most of the energy pours out as fast neutrons that bombard the walls, activate the structure, and force a lifetime of shielding and replacement. The cathedral gets built, and it teaches us the physics, but it is not, by itself, a template for a cheap, mass-produced, clean power plant. It was never trying to be. It was trying to prove the plasma physics for all of humanity, and at that it has largely, magnificently, succeeded.

The compact-tokamak wave

The second family is the one most people picture when they hear "private fusion," and it is the one that broke the field's long spell of waiting. Over the last decade a wave of privately funded efforts has taken the tokamak — the same fundamentally sound doughnut — and asked a sharp, almost impudent question: what if the reason tokamaks have to be so cathedral-sized is simply that their magnets are too weak? Make the magnetic field strong enough and the whole machine can shrink, because confinement improves steeply as the field rises — steeply enough that a modest gain in magnet strength buys a dramatic cut in machine size.

The enabling technology behind this wave is high-temperature superconducting tape — a magnet material that can carry enormous current density and sustain very high fields in a compact coil. It is a genuine breakthrough, one of the real ones, and it changed what is possible for everyone, my own team emphatically included. The strength of this family is speed and capital efficiency of a kind the cathedral projects can never have: smaller machines, faster build cycles, private funding that moves at the pace of conviction rather than treaty, and a credible argument that a commercially relevant tokamak can be built in years rather than decades. I have enormous respect for this wave. It broke the assumption that fusion must always be enormous and always be slow, and it did so with real physics rather than slogans — which, in this field, is the highest compliment I know how to pay.

But this family, for all its speed, still makes one foundational choice that carries a cost it cannot design away: it still burns deuterium and tritium. A high-field compact tokamak is a smaller, faster machine, but it is still, in the end, a machine that produces most of its energy as fast neutrons. The neutron flux, concentrated in a smaller volume, is if anything more punishing per unit of wall — the same fire in a smaller hearth burns the bricks hotter. So the same hard questions return, and they do not go away because the machine is elegant: how long do the materials last, how radioactive does the structure become, how often must components be swapped, and what does all of that do to the cost of a delivered megawatt-hour. These are not reasons to doubt the approach. They are the honest homework the approach still has in front of it, and the best people in it will tell you the same, without flinching.

Strong magnets made the tokamak small. They did not make the neutron go away.

Laser and inertial confinement

The third family takes a completely different path to the same star — a path so different it barely looks like the same field. Instead of holding a thin plasma in place with magnets for a long time, it takes a tiny pellet of fuel and crushes it — with a colossal, precisely timed pulse of laser light or other driver energy — so fast and so hard that it fuses in a flash before it can fly apart. Magnetic confinement holds a diffuse plasma steady for seconds; inertial confinement lets the fuel's own inertia hold it together for the single nanosecond that matters, and in that nanosecond lights a star the size of a peppercorn.

This family earned the field's most famous single result: the laboratory demonstration that a fusion reaction can release more energy than the driver delivered to the fuel capsule itself. That was a real and historic threshold, a line humanity had never crossed, and it silenced a certain kind of doubt for good. The strength here is that the physics of ignition — the actual lighting of the fire — has been demonstrated in a way that is very hard to argue with, and the approach sidesteps the steady-state confinement problem entirely by not trying to hold anything steady at all.

The weakness is the vast gap between a spectacular single shot and a power plant that runs your city. A plant must do this not once but many times a second, every second, for years on end. It must manufacture flawless fuel capsules at enormous volume and low cost, fire drivers that are efficient enough that the plant produces far more energy than the whole facility consumes — not just more than reached the capsule, which is a very different and much harder ledger — and survive the repeated micro-explosions at its heart without shaking itself to pieces. Each of those is a formidable engineering program in its own right, any one of which could consume a decade. The fire has been lit, and that is no small thing. Turning a controlled series of tiny explosions into a dispatchable generator is the long road that remains, and the people walking it know exactly, unsentimentally, how long it is.

The alternative concepts

The fourth family is not one approach but a whole teeming ecosystem of them — the configurations that are neither the mainstream tokamak nor the laser. I group them together not because they are alike, for they are not, but because each represents a bet that the dominant path left something valuable on the table, some door the crowd walked past.

There are the mirror machines: straight magnetic bottles that trap plasma between high-field magnetic plugs at each end, rather than bending it into a ring. Their appeal is geometric simplicity, natural suitability for steady operation, and an openness to fuels and conversion schemes that a closed doughnut resists; their historic difficulty was holding the plasma against losses out the open ends. There are the stellarators: tokamak cousins that twist the confining field with intricately shaped external coils — sculptures of wire and math — instead of relying on a current driven through the plasma. They trade fearsome manufacturing complexity for the great prize of intrinsically steady, disruption-resistant operation. There are the field-reversed configurations and other compact-toroid schemes: elegant, self-organized plasma rings that carry their own field and promise very high efficiency in a small volume, if their stability and confinement can be tamed. And there are the pinches and their modern descendants, which use the plasma's own currents to squeeze and confine it, chasing radical simplicity and low cost — betting that clever physics can do the work of expensive magnets.

The shared strength of this family is imagination disciplined by physics — the best kind, the kind that dreams inside the rules. Each of these concepts exists because someone looked hard at a real limitation of the mainstream and asked whether a different geometry could dissolve it rather than fight it. The shared weakness is maturity: they have, in general, far less cumulative experimental time behind them than the mainstream tokamak, so more of their key questions remain open, more of their promises untested. That is a reason for humility, not dismissal. More than once in the history of technology, the approach that looked "behind" turned out to be behind on funding and attention, not on merit — waiting, like a mirror waiting for the right fuel, for its moment to arrive.

Where our approach sits

Now I can place our own work honestly, because you can only understand a design by the company it keeps and the company it deliberately leaves behind.

We build two machines, not one. A breeder — a compact spherical tokamak that burns deuterium and tritium — and a burner — a tandem-mirror generator that burns deuterium and helium-3. I have told the story elsewhere in this book of why the physics forced us to split the job in two, why one machine could not honestly be both foundry and power plant; here I only want to locate that choice on the map I have just drawn, and to be candid about what is borrowed and what is genuinely, defensibly different.

Look at the breeder and you will see how much we owe the other families — how little of it is ours alone. It is a tokamak, which means it stands on the half-century of plasma physics the great public machines paid for in money and patience. It is a compact tokamak wound with high-temperature superconducting magnets — its design basis carries a very high peak field in the coil — which means it rides the very same superconducting wave that the private compact-tokamak family opened up for all of us. We did not invent that road. We are grateful to be on it. If those families had not done their work, ours would be flatly impossible; we would be dreaming, not building.

Look at the burner and you will see the debt to the alternative-concepts family, the debt to the road less travelled. It is a tandem mirror — a straight magnetic bottle with high-field end plugs, reaching a peak field near 26.49 tesla at the plug — a direct descendant of the mirror lineage that the mainstream once set aside as a dead end. We picked it up not out of nostalgia, not to rescue an old idea for sentiment's sake, but because, once you decide to burn a clean fuel, the open geometry is the right shape for the job in a way the closed doughnut simply is not.

It is worth saying why the shape follows from the fuel, because this is the crux of the whole two-machine logic and the place where the design stops being an assembly of borrowed parts and becomes an argument. Deuterium and helium-3 is a much harder reaction to ignite than deuterium and tritium — it wants higher temperatures, and it rewards you, in exchange for that difficulty, with energy carried by charged particles rather than neutrons. Now follow the logic where it leads: if your fuel's payoff is charged particles, you want a machine whose geometry lets you catch those particles and steer them toward electricity directly, and an open-ended magnetic bottle does exactly that. The charged exhaust streams out the ends, straight into a direct-conversion train, instead of being trapped forever circling a closed ring where its energy can only be harvested as heat. The mirror's historic weakness — that plasma leaks out the ends — becomes, for this fuel, the very feature you want, provided you can plug the ends hard enough with high-field magnets to hold the plasma long enough to burn. That is what the tandem mirror's end plugs are for, and it is why the burner reaches for such extreme fields at its throats. The mainstream set the mirror aside decades ago because, for the easy D–T fuel, a closed torus confined better — and they were right, for that fuel. We picked it back up because, for the clean fuel we actually want to burn, the mirror's open geometry is not a handicap to be overcome but the shape the physics is quietly asking for. The lineage was never wrong. It was waiting for the fuel that suited it, the way a key waits in a drawer for the lock it fits.

So what actually diverges? Four things, and I want to name each one plainly and without varnish, because they are the substance of the bet — the part that is genuinely ours.

What we diverge on

First: fuel before power. Almost every other effort in every family is trying, ultimately, to build a machine that makes electricity, because electricity is the prize everyone can see. We decided the near-term product of fusion is not electricity at all — it is fuel and materials. Our breeder is a foundry, not a power station. Its job is to make tritium, to make helium-3, and to pour out 14-MeV neutrons that have real industrial value, with its tritium loop held deliberately just above replacement (breeding lever 1.03–1.20). I will say the uncomfortable part out loud, as I do throughout this book because burying it would poison everything else: the breeder is net-negative on electricity — on the order of tens of megawatts in the red. That is not a defect we are hiding in a footnote. It is the design, chosen on purpose. We chose to build the fuel factory first and let it fund the power plant, rather than demand that one machine be both at once and be brilliant at neither. Most of the field is betting on the power plant. We are betting that whoever owns the fuel owns the decade before the power plants arrive — and that owning a decade is worth more than owning a headline.

Second: a genuinely low-neutron burn. The mainstream tokamak and the entire compact-tokamak wave burn deuterium and tritium and inherit the neutron in full, with all its slow violence to the walls. We push the neutron problem upstream into the breeder — where we want neutrons, where neutrons are the whole point and the product — and keep the burner clean. The burner's deuterium–helium-3 reaction runs at a neutron fraction of only about 5.44 percent, a small fraction of what D–T produces. That is the difference between a power plant that slowly destroys its own walls, tithing itself to the neutron year after year, and one that does not. It is the oldest dream in fusion, aneutronic-leaning power, the dream the field has chased since its youth — and we reach for it not by wishing the neutron away inside a single heroic machine but by dividing the labor between two, sending the neutrons where they are welcome.

Third: direct conversion. Because the burner's energy comes out mostly as charged particles rather than neutrons, we can catch that energy and turn it toward electricity directly — collecting the current at the source — rather than boiling water and running a steam turbine the way nearly every thermal plant on Earth still does: fission, coal, gas, and most fusion designs alike, all of them, at bottom, elaborate kettles. Direct energy conversion is not available to a machine whose output is chiefly fast neutrons; it is a prize you can only claim if you have first committed to a clean, charged-particle fuel. It is a divergence that only becomes possible because of the first two — one good choice unlocking the next, the way real design compounds.

Fourth: a deliberately conservative timeline. This is the least glamorous divergence and, I have come to believe, the most important of all four. Much of the field — understandably, under the relentless pressure of funding and enthusiasm and the human hunger for good news — reaches for the nearest credible date it can defend. We do the opposite, on purpose and against our own short-term interest. Our public promise is framed within forty years, with an internal plan that lands earlier, precisely so that we are structurally unable to over-promise even if we wanted to. The staged-road chapter lays out the full ladder of dates — design closed now, first breeder construction, first tritium, the first test burner, a commercial burner fleet, and the arrival of lunar helium-3 that finally opens the fuel economics — and I will not restate that ladder here; what matters for the map is that every rung of it is set later than the most optimistic version I could sell you if I were trying to sell you something. That is on purpose. Under-promising is not modesty, and it is not timidity. It is a design constraint, load-bearing as any magnet.

The magnet, the common inheritance

Before I state the bets, I want to dwell on the one piece of technology that runs underneath nearly every modern approach on this map, ours included, because it is the clearest example of how little of this grand enterprise is any one team's private achievement — how much of it is a gift we all inherited.

Everything fast and compact in fusion today rides on high-temperature superconducting tape. The old assumption — the one that made the great public tokamaks so vast, so cathedral-slow — was that magnetic fields were limited by what conventional superconductors could sustain, and since confinement improves steeply with field, weak fields forced enormous machines. High-temperature superconductor broke that assumption clean in half. It carries enormous current density and holds very high fields in a compact coil, and it changed the possibility space for everyone at once, the way a single new material occasionally reorganizes an entire field of engineering. The compact-tokamak wave exists because of it. Our breeder exists because of it: its design basis runs 8 tesla on-axis with a far higher peak in the coil, at a size that would have been simply unreachable a generation ago, the stuff of viewgraphs and wishes. Our burner leans on it even harder, reaching toward a peak field near 26.49 tesla at the end plugs, because a tandem mirror lives or dies on how hard you can squeeze the plasma at its throats.

I dwell on this because it is the honest posture of the whole chapter in miniature, the thesis compressed into a coil of tape. We did not invent the tape. We did not invent the tokamak, or the mirror, or the physics of the burning plasma. We are standing on an inheritance that the public machines, the private wave, and the materials scientists built — standing on shoulders, as the old phrase has it, though the people whose shoulders they are will mostly go unthanked by history. The most our design can claim is to have arranged those inherited pieces into a configuration nobody else chose to arrange them in. A design that pretended otherwise — that dressed up a shared enabling technology as a proprietary breakthrough, that claimed the inheritance as invention — would be exactly the kind of design I told you at the outset I would not trust with a match. The magnet is common ground. What we did with it is the only thing that is ours, and it is enough.

The software machine

There is a fifth divergence I left out of the four above, because it does not fit the geometry-and-fuel frame of the others, and it is where I am willing to make the strongest near-term claim in this entire book — the one place I will let myself sound certain. Most of the field treats control software as an accessory to the physics, a technician bolted on after the real work. We treat it as part of the machine, as load-bearing as the magnets.

A fusion plasma is a violently nonlinear system that must be held at a hundred million degrees inside a magnetic cage, and it fails fast — disruptions and instabilities can develop in milliseconds, far faster than any human operator can even perceive, let alone react to. The traditional answer is hand-tuned control and conservative operating margins, a human hand kept nervously near the switch. Ours is a machine-learning control layer, and unlike the quantum-computing promises the field is so fond of making, this is not a someday capability waiting on a breakthrough. It works now, and it works with numbers I can state and stand behind — the safety clamp, for one, caught every one of three thousand injected limit violations, with zero escapes. I will not reprint the whole ledger here; the AI chapter carries the full receipts — the surrogate speed-ups, the disruption scores, the quench-precursor warnings, and, in the same discipline, the honest misses set down beside the wins.

I keep that discipline here too — every claim shown with its shortfall beside it, because a control layer you cannot check is a control layer you should not believe. The point, in a chapter about where we fit, is that this is a genuine, measurable advantage available today, on hardware that does not yet exist for the plasma but exists entirely for the software — and it is developed with the one external partner named in this book, NVIDIA, whose accelerators run these models. That is a real thing, running now, while the rest of the machine is still being built.

And because I am on the subject of computation, let me repeat the honesty the rest of the field so often skips past when the applause is loudest: quantum computing offers this program no near-term and no near-decade advantage, and I say so plainly, against the constant temptation to imply otherwise and borrow the glamour. What is real is quantum sensing for diagnostics, which is genuinely near and genuinely useful, and quantum-inspired tensor methods that run on ordinary hardware today. The divergence that matters is not a quantum fantasy dressed for a keynote; it is a classical, working, numbers-on-the-table control machine. Treating software as a first-class part of the reactor, rather than a bolt-on afterthought, is a quieter divergence than fuel or geometry — but it is the one already paying off, already earning its place, already real.

What we are betting that others are not

Strip away the machines and the map and the borrowed magnets, and every approach in fusion reduces to a single bet — a wager about which hard problem is the one worth building your whole strategy, your whole company, your whole life around. So let me state ours as plainly as I can, and grant at once, before you can say it, that it may be wrong.

We are betting that the binding constraint on fusion is not, in the end, the plasma. The great public machines are close to settling the plasma physics; the compact-tokamak wave is bringing the magnets; ignition itself has been demonstrated in a laboratory. The plasma, I have come to believe, will be solved — by the field, collectively, sooner than the skeptics believe and perhaps sooner than some of its own champions fear. We are betting that once the plasma is solved, the real constraint, the one left standing when the famous problem falls, becomes materials and fuel: what survives the neutron flux year after year, where the tritium and helium-3 actually come from at scale, and whether the delivered electron is cheap enough to matter to anyone. That is a bet on chemistry and metallurgy and supply chains as much as on physics — an unromantic bet, a bet on the unglamorous back rooms of the enterprise, and a deliberate one made with eyes open.

We are betting, second, that being first to fuel is worth more in the near term than being first to a single triumphant demonstration of net electric power — that a foundry which earns its keep selling materials can fund the slow, patient work of the power fleet, while efforts staking everything on one triumphant power milestone are more fragile than they look under the stage lights, one bad shot away from a crisis.

And we are betting, third, on being boring about time. In a field where the temptation to promise the nearest date is nearly irresistible, where every year brings a new "fusion in a decade," we are betting that the effort which under-promises and compounds quietly, unglamorously, without spending its credibility on a headline, outlives the ones that spend theirs early and loudly.

We are not betting the plasma is hardest. We are betting the plasma gets solved — and that materials, fuel, and honesty about time are what is left.

I could be wrong about all three, and I want that possibility on the record in my own hand. The compact-tokamak wave could reach clean, cheap power on deuterium and tritium faster than I expect, and make our fuel-first patience look like overcaution dressed as wisdom. Ignition could scale to a working inertial plant before our burner fleet is built. One of the alternative concepts I described with such fondness could turn out to have quietly solved the very problem it was long doubted on, in some laboratory not making headlines. If any of that happens, it is a win for the thing all of us actually care about, the thing under all the rivalry — clean power for everyone, for good — and I will be genuinely glad of it, even if it is not our machine that gets there first. That gladness is not a pose. It is the only sane way to feel about a prize this large.

That is the honest map, and the honest posture that goes with it. I have tried to draw every road fairly, without a thumb on the scale for my own, because every road is being walked by people who deserve fairness and because a design that can only look good by making its neighbours look bad is not a design worth your trust or mine. Ours is one road among several good ones, on a plain wide enough for all of them. What follows in this book is simply the case, laid out with the numbers shown and the misses printed, for why I believe it is a road worth building — not the only one, and not a certain one, but an honest one, and, I have staked my life on the wager, a road that reaches the star.

A Brighter Tomorrow

Come forward with me — not to a date I will promise you, because the honesty of this book is worth more than the drama of a year, but to the world that waits on the other side of a single number. Stand in it for a while. Walk its streets, drink its water, breathe its air. Everything you are about to see is downstream of two small, stubborn things, and I will hold them in front of you the whole way so the vision never floats free of them.

The first is a price: forty dollars a megawatt-hour — the line below which firm, carbon-free electricity stops being a premium good and becomes something closer to air, cheap enough that you stop rationing it and stop building your life around its scarcity. The second is a property, and it is the one the whole book was built to earn: firmness — power that runs day and night, in still air and cloud, through polar winter and monsoon, without ever once asking permission of the weather. Cheap intermittent power changes the electricity bill. Cheap firm power changes what you can build, and therefore what a human life can be.

I will not let the vision drift loose of its gate, because that drift is exactly how every earlier generation of this dream curdled into a broken promise. None of what follows arrives the morning a machine switches on. The burner fleet that delivers power at this price is years of hard engineering away, and one of its cheapest routes is gated — as the earlier chapters said plainly, and I will not now un-say it — on lunar helium-3 that does not yet exist at scale, which is precisely why the breeder, Hyperion, is designed to make helium-3 on Earth in the meantime, so the burner is never left staring at the sky, waiting. So read what follows as a map of consequences, not a set of promises. It is the answer to the only question that ever justified the decades of work and the honest years of doubt: if we succeed, what is it for?

This is what it is for.

The morning the water stopped being a wall

Begin where scarcity has drawn blood longest: at the tap. For most of history a city in a dry country woke to the oldest question there is — where does the water come from? — and the answer was a river it did not control or an aquifer it was mining toward empty. But the sea was always right there, the largest reservoir on the planet, and the only thing standing between the city and it was energy. The membranes work today; you can walk through the plants. The thermodynamic floor for pulling fresh water from seawater is a little over a kilowatt-hour a cubic metre, and real plants spend three or four. That gap — not chemistry, not the membrane, only the price of the electron pushed through it — was the whole wall.

Watch firmness take the wall down. A desalination plant is capital-intensive machinery that hates to stop; its membranes resent being cycled, and every idle hour is expensive metal depreciating for nothing. Pair it with an intermittent source and it waits three-quarters of the year for the sun. Pair it with a generator that runs by nature and it runs by nature too — and the match between a continuous process and a continuous generator is the entire reason the water comes out cheap. Below the forty-dollar line the arithmetic simply inverts: the machine that was too expensive to run without stopping becomes the cheapest source of water the city has, and the city stops rationing and simply chooses to drink the sea, the way it chooses to build a bridge.

And the choice ripples outward the moment it is made. The hot, hypersaline brine that plants once fought to dump becomes an ore body — lithium and magnesium worth separating now that the chemistry pays for itself. Ancient aquifers under northern India and the North China Plain and the American West, drained in decades that took millennia to fill, become batteries instead of graves, recharged with power that no longer has to be hoarded. Ultrapure water — the kind a semiconductor fab and an electrolyser cannot live without — turns abundant where it was precious. And a nation that can make its own fresh water from the ocean negotiates its shared rivers from security rather than desperation, turning a knife-edge over a fixed river into a solvable question of who builds which plant. Water was the first hostage scarcity ever took. A cheap, tireless electron is how you ransom it back.

The bread of the air, and the forge that stops smoking

Follow the water inland and it becomes food, because behind every calorie is a hidden river and, one step further back, a hidden current of energy. Roughly half the people alive were, in a strict and literal sense, grown from natural gas: the Haber–Bosch process marries nitrogen from the air to hydrogen cracked out of methane, and it feeds the world while quietly venting the carbon of that feeding into the sky. You cannot switch it off. You can only change what feeds it — and the change is a single swap at the very front of the line. Split the hydrogen from water with cheap firm electricity instead of from gas, and the century-old reaction that grows half the world's food stops being a fossil enterprise. The nitrogen is already free, four-fifths of every breath. The molecule that comes out is identical. Only its history is clean. The bread, from now on, is baked out of the air.
