Now stand the same electrolyser beside the same generator and feed it the other way, and it becomes the hinge of an entire industrial civilisation learning to make things without fire. Iron ore is rust — iron locked to oxygen — and for three centuries we tore the two apart the only way we knew, with carbon: `2 Fe₂O₃ + 3 C → 4 Fe + 3 CO₂`, every tonne of iron trailing nearly two tonnes of carbon dioxide, a fourteenth of all human emissions printed into the sky straight out of the chemistry. There is another reductant that does the same job and leaves only water: hydrogen. Run `Fe₂O₃ + 3 H₂ → 2 Fe + 3 H₂O`, melt the sponge iron in an electric arc furnace, and steel walks out clean. The route is not speculative; direct-reduced iron is made at scale today. What kept it a demonstration was the hydrogen — and what turns green steel from a subsidised showpiece into the default way to make the metal that builds the fusion plants themselves is firm power, the kind that keeps the expensive electrolyser working every hour of the year rather than idling for the calm. The gate is real and I will name it: furnaces retrofitted, hydrogen stored and handled, none of it free. But the physics is settled. The only fire steel still needs is the one we choose to light.

And what happens to steel happens across the whole forge of the modern world, because nearly a third of global emissions come not from cars or homes but from the heat and chemistry of making things — and a factory needs its power unwavering, since a single flicker can scrap a whole shift at a fab that then takes days to recover. Cement gets clean process heat and affordable capture for the carbon the limestone itself exhales. Aluminium — electricity stored in metal — stops chasing the few places with cheap hydropower and settles wherever a compact generator can stand. The copper and lithium and rare earths a green economy runs on stop being mined by burning the very thing they are meant to replace. The recycled tonne quietly becomes the cheaper tonne, and the circular economy becomes plain economics rather than a virtue. Chemicals and plastics build themselves from captured carbon and split water, the petroleum left in the ground. One boiler, one furnace, one smelter at a time, the smoke goes out of the making of things — not by asking anyone to make less, but by changing what the making runs on.

The thinking machines, fed at last

There is a reason a fusion company and an artificial-intelligence company find themselves talking, and it is not fashion. Modern AI is, physically, a machine for turning electricity into inference, and it has run headlong into the wall that electricity is neither cheap, firm, nor clean enough to feed its appetite. A hyperscale computing campus does not breathe like a city; it does not dip at midnight or slump on a holiday. It draws the same vast power at three in the morning as at noon, every day of the year — a flat line on the chart, the purest firm load our economy has ever built. And the brutal arithmetic of serving a flat line is that the cheapest way to feed it is with a generator that produces one, not with a fluctuating source propped up on batteries sized for the worst still night of the year.

This is why one of the burner's housings, MetroVolt, is built to stand at the fence line of the campus rather than at the far end of a transmission corridor. In more and more regions the true limit on where computation can grow is no longer the chips or the capital but the interconnection queue — the years-long wait for permission to draw from a grid that has run out of room. A firm source behind the meter changes what "possible to build here" even means, and does it without lighting a molecule of gas. Freed from chasing the few places with spare capacity, the data centres scatter to where the users are, or the cold climates, or the industries they serve — and the great simulations ride the same abundance: climate, drug discovery, protein folding, materials, all limited today by how much compute a lab can afford. There is even a loop that closes on itself, and I find it quietly astonishing: this very machine was designed with large-scale simulation and AI surrogates, so cheaper computation makes the next hard machine easier to design than this one was.

And there is a deeper symmetry, the one that made the partnership inevitable. The machine that would feed the thinking machines is itself run by a thinking machine. The burner is a plasma at conditions no human reflex could govern; the control stack — built with NVIDIA, the one external partner named in this book — runs surrogate models up to three orders of magnitude faster than direct calculation, a magnet twin some seven-thousand-fold quicker, so a controller can rehearse the next microsecond before it arrives. Its fused early-warning system reads a coming disruption forty-seven milliseconds out where a single diagnostic would offer barely two and a half; a safety clamp caught every one of three thousand injected limit violations across a hundred and fifty thousand steps, with zero escapes. Artificial intelligence does not make the plasma burn hotter. It makes a burning plasma governable — which is the precondition under a generator you would dare to site beside the racks it powers. (I keep one discipline here against the field's habit: fusion needs no quantum computer, and quantum computing offers this work no near-decade advantage. What is genuinely near is quantum sensing for diagnostics — the honest part, named as such.)

The world set in motion

You do not put a reactor in a car, and I will not pretend otherwise. But nearly every clean way to move people and goods is, underneath, a way of delivering electricity — and its price and firmness decide whether the clean option wins. The reactor never leaves the ground; it just makes the electrons, the hydrogen, and the synthetic fuel cheap enough to finally choose over what we burn. The electric fleet charges heaviest at two in the morning, when the sun is long gone and the honest match is not another solar panel but a source that is simply there. Freight rail's long-life arithmetic tips off diesel the moment the price of power over the line stays low and firm. And for the machines too heavy, too far, too fast for a battery — the ship crossing an ocean, the aircraft eight miles up — the answer comes out of the air itself.

A wing cares about energy per kilogram, and aviation fuel packs some forty-three megajoules into every one, which is why long-haul flight will want a dense liquid for a long time yet. It can come out of the air. Take carbon dioxide — from a flue or from the sky — and hydrogen split from water, build them back into a synthetic crude, and refine a jet fuel chemically indistinguishable from the fossil kind, the carbon out of the engine only the carbon that went in. The chemistry is old and proven; its entire cost is the energy poured into making it. Drop that below the line and hold it there, and clean flight crosses from gesture to supply. The same chain, one branch earlier, fuels the sea:

Link in the chainWhat it needs to be cheap
Firm clean electricitythe generator that runs by nature
Green hydrogenthat electricity, and an electrolyser kept busy
Ammonia / methanol / syncrudethat hydrogen, plus captured carbon or free nitrogen
A ship or a plane refuelled cleanall of the above holding at once

A generator standing on land quietly decides what a ship burns in the middle of the ocean, and what an aircraft burns over the pole. Every hard-to-electrify machine we have waits at the end of a chain whose first link is a cheap, firm electron.

The healing

Not every gift of these machines is measured in megawatts. Some are measured in the vials a hospital's nuclear-medicine department opens each morning — and, wider by far, in the plain fact of reliable power where there has never been any. More lives turn on a clinic that keeps its lights and its refrigerators running than on any exotic isotope, and I will not let the rare thing crowd out the common one.

But the rare thing is real. The breeder makes its fuel by flooding its blanket with the hardest neutrons fusion throws — 14-MeV neutrons, with a breeding lever above one, replacing the fuel it burns — and a neutron source that prolific is, almost incidentally, one of the most useful instruments a country can own. The isotope behind tens of millions of cardiac and cancer scans a year hangs today on a handful of ageing reactors, any one of which going down for repairs can ripple into a shortage that reaches the patient on the table. Slide the right target into the flux and the same neutrons that breed tritium in one part of the blanket breed medicine in another. And helium-3 — which the breeder co-produces, and which the burner will one day crave from the Moon — is prized here and now for lung imaging and ultra-cold refrigeration, its supply eked today from the slow decay of aged warheads, which is no way to run a hospital. The fuel cycle, it turns out, has a bedside manner. Around all of it stands the humbler mercy: the clinic refrigerator that stops failing at the worst possible second, the operating theatre whose power does not flicker mid-procedure, the cold chain whose gap simply never opens — the hour that never goes dark.

The repair

Firm clean power is the largest single lever on emissions ever placed within human reach, because so much of what warms the planet is simply the burning of fuel for energy — and the largest, least glamorous move of all is switching one plant off and another on. Here most clean alternatives quietly fail the interview. A coal plant promises power on a windless week in January; a solar farm with a battery can chase that promise but cannot make it. Firmness is the whole difference between a substitute and a supplement. A firm, dispatchable, carbon-free generator does not sit beside the retiring coal plant hedged with batteries — it takes the plant's place on the grid diagram, same node, same reliability, same always-there, and simply stops emitting. Along the burner's roughly four-hundred-and-forty-metre axis, magnets reaching a peak near twenty-six and a half tesla in the end plugs hold a plasma in a bottle with no ends to leak through, burning deuterium and helium-3 at a neutron fraction near five and a half percent and converting much of its output directly rather than by boiling water — which is why it drinks so little cooling water and throws off so little waste heat. The point of all that engineering is one unremarkable virtue: it is there, all the time, on purpose. And that virtue is what finally lets a grid switch off the gas "peaker" kept breathing in reserve behind even the greenest-looking system — not overbuilt, not over-stored, not hedged. Replaced.

Then, beyond retiring the fire, the harder work: taking back some of what we already put up. Direct air capture pulls carbon dioxide straight out of an atmosphere where it is only four parts in ten thousand — un-mixing the sky, thermodynamically expensive, which is the single reason it has stayed a boutique affair measured in thousands of tonnes against a problem measured in billions. Firm fusion power attacks that expense from both sides: cheap enough to run continuously until the numbers close, and clean enough that the cure is not worse than the disease, because capture run on dirty power can emit more than it removes. I keep this one honest, because it is the item most easily oversold: direct air capture is not permission to keep emitting. It is the slow, expensive repair for what could not be prevented, and it earns its place only after the cheaper move — retiring the fossil plant — is made. But a warming world will need repair, and for the first time the medicine we always knew how to make becomes something we can also afford to take, at the dose the wound requires. Around it, the rest of the repair we long knew how to do and never could afford: degraded land greened with cheap desalinated water, legacy pollution finally cleaned rather than fenced off, carbon turned back into stone by enhanced weathering, and — the quiet giant — high-yield indoor farms and water drawn from the sea shrinking the human footprint so that abundance for people and room for everything else stop being a cruel trade.

The city, and the places that must never go dark

A city is a machine for concentrating people, and everything about it — water, heat, transport, air — is downstream of the price and reliability of energy. For the first time the generator can be a good neighbour rather than a distant, dirty thing kept over the horizon: built compact and clean, the burner can sit near the demand it serves, cutting the losses of long transmission and freeing the grid from a single fragile artery one storm can sever. It anchors a microgrid that "islands" — that disconnects from a failing grid and keeps a hospital or a water plant alive on the worst day of the year, not the average one. It electrifies the buildings whose heating peaks on the coldest, darkest winter nights, exactly when the sun is weakest and only firm winter power will do. And within a few years of the combustion leaving a city's power, heat, and transport, the air over it changes measurably — felt in every pair of lungs, the youngest and the oldest first.

And because firm power is, at bottom, a strategic asset, no honest telling would leave out the places someone is actively trying to switch off. One of the burner's housings — Aegis — is built for exactly this, and I state it plainly rather than tuck it away, because the same firmness that runs a data centre runs a base, and pretending otherwise would be an evasion I have promised not to commit. A base, a radar station, a command centre guarantees its power today with fields of diesel fed by slow, vulnerable convoys; a compact generator on site removes both the emissions and the ambush, because the convoy that never rolls cannot be attacked. The same logic hardens the civilian infrastructure — water, hospitals, communications — whose deepest shared vulnerability is the grid, turning one fragile network into many resilient cells that fail, if at all, one at a time rather than all at once in a cascade. And a nation that makes its own tritium, helium-3, and medical isotopes from a breeder it controls no longer has to ask anyone's permission for the scarce materials a modern state runs on. Development has always been rationed by the price of power. Lower it for everyone, and you widen the circle of who gets to build a future.

The circle widened

This is where cheap firm power does its most human work, and where I hold myself hardest to honesty, because infrastructure is slow and political and reaches the poorest last, whatever the physics allows and however fiercely I wish it otherwise. Strip away the machines and the vision, and energy poverty is simply poverty wearing another name. Something close to the population of a whole continent still lives without reliable electricity — not without any power, often, but without the boring, dependable, always-there kind you can build a life on top of.

So watch a region get it, because the transformation is made of small, unglamorous mercies compounding. The clinic's refrigerator stops failing, so the vaccines survive the hot end of the line. The pump runs when the field needs it, so the farmer plants for yield instead of gambling the whole season on the rains. The workshop keeps its full hours, and the wage that comes with them. A child reads after dark by a steady bulb instead of a kerosene lamp that is dim, dear, and dangerous to breathe beside — and the hours that adds to a childhood compound, over years, into something no aid programme can buy directly. Clean water arrives through the main rather than the pharmacy, and does more preventive medicine than any pill. The daily regressive tax the poorest pay — kerosene, charcoal, diesel when the grid is down, a premium charged simply for being poor — lifts. None of it asks for a scientific miracle. It asks for the humblest thing on this whole list: power that is simply, boringly, there.

And standing behind every one of these, the largest freedom of all and the quietest — the one the rest depend on. So much of geopolitics is a scramble over fuels: who holds them, who controls the routes, who can be cut off in a hard winter. Energy generated anywhere, from fuel drawn ultimately from seawater and the Moon, drains that poison from the well of international relations. I no longer write, as I once did, that this makes peace inevitable — that was a young writer's word, and honesty is the currency of this book. Abundant, siteable, everyone-can-make-it energy does not guarantee peace. It does something more modest and, in the long arc, more durable: it dissolves one of the oldest and most reliable reasons human beings have ever had to fight. It removes a driver. It does not remove them all — and the distance between those two sentences is the distance between a slogan and an argument I can defend without flinching.

The frontier

And then, because the same energy density that runs a city can run a world, the story leaves the ground — and here I keep the caveat at full strength, without apology, because almost all of this lies further off than everything above, and some of it very much further, past the edge of what this book can promise. The Moon keeps the most unforgiving schedule in the inner solar system: fourteen Earth-days of sunlight, then fourteen of dark. A solar panel is dead weight through every hour of that fortnight-long night, and it is this — more than radiation or dust or distance — that quietly kills most designs for a permanent base on the drawing board. A settlement either carries its own firm power across the dark or it freezes solid in it, and there is no third option and no one to call. A compact fusion generator runs straight through the long night: firmness in its most literal form, where the alternative to power is not inconvenience but death.

And once there is power to spare on the surface, the loop closes in a way I still find astonishing. Lunar regolith holds helium-3, salted in grain by grain over billions of years of solar wind, and baking it out means heating vast tonnages of soil — which takes energy, which the generator supplies. Fusion power helps mine the very fuel that fusion power runs on. I will say the gate one final time, plainly: this is an unproven, off-world programme near the bottom of the readiness ladder, the single gate on which the burner's cheapest power waits — which is exactly why the breeder matters so much here and now, making helium-3 on Earth while the Moon is still a plan on paper, so the burner is never left waiting on the sky. Beyond that lie the nearer frontiers I will name but not oversell — ice split into propellant so a mission need not haul every gram up from the bottom of Earth's gravity well, orbital depots kept cold, factories in free fall — and, at the very top of the speculation ladder, generations away and beyond anything in these pages, the dirtiest industry lifted off a living planet altogether, and a propulsion that could turn months of travel into weeks. Naming the distance is not the same as denying the direction. Fusion should not be the reason humanity goes to the Moon. It should be a patient customer of a cislunar economy built for other reasons — a demand signal specific enough to help pull the infrastructure into being, and disciplined enough to wait for it rather than pretend it is already there.

What the fire is for

I promised a map of consequences, not a set of promises, and I will end by keeping that promise about promises. Notice the kind of world I have just walked you through, because its character is the whole argument. Almost nothing in it required a scientific miracle or an undiscovered law. Desalination works today; it is merely priced out. So does direct air capture, green steel, clean hydrogen, indoor farming, electric everything — the science is largely done, sitting on the shelf, and the single dominant term keeping it there marked too expensive is the cost of a firm kilowatt-hour. And I have tried, scene by scene, to keep the exceptions in plain view: the frontiers genuinely far off, the places where firmness matters more than price, the ones where cheap energy helps only at the margins and human habit or politics or taste must do the rest.

So this was never a hundred separate bets scattered across a table. It is one bet, made a hundred times over — a single wager wearing a hundred faces. Push the price of firm, clean power below the line and hold it there, and the shelf comes down: not everywhere at once, not on any date I will promise you, but steadily, city after city and field after field, as the arithmetic quietly inverts. What separates this book from the one I first wrote in 2024 is not that I have grown more certain the vision is nice — anyone can love a vision. It is that I now have a closed, published design and an honest, staged plan for reaching the price, with every gate named out loud, including the ones that lie outside our control and behind which the cheapest power patiently waits.

Energy is water. Energy is food. Energy is health, and clean air, and computation, and the freedom not to have your survival held hostage by geography or the weather or the price of a distant barrel. Energy is freedom — and here were more than a hundred of its shapes, and behind every one of them the same quiet, stubborn, honest machine, doing the one thing that changes all the rest.

This chapter's forty. All three at once — Q40, $40 a megawatt-hour, within forty years — because every door in this brighter tomorrow opens only when the physics, the price, and the clock are kept together.

How This Was Built

The physics in this book is solved. But a solved physics is not a company, a company is not a machine, and none of it builds itself. Behind every equation in these pages is a person who checked it, an argument that took years to win, and a great deal that had nothing to do with plasma at all. This chapter is about that — the people who gave the work its shape, and the honest fact that assembling them was harder than any calculation in the book. Part I told you who these people are and why the century's streams converge in them; this chapter tells the lived version — how it actually happened, email by unanswered email.

I came to fusion by an unlikely road, and I have never tried to hide it. I am not a physicist by training. What I had, at the start, was a conviction inherited from my family, a habit of building things learned in industry, and a willingness to send my work to people far more expert than I was and ask them, plainly, whether it held. Much of what follows began exactly that way — as unsolicited email into inboxes I had no claim on.

The twins who answered

Some of the most consequential relationships of my life began as emails I wasn't sure anyone would answer. In the suspended year of 2020, with the world shut indoors, I started mailing mathematical proofs of fusion-energy designs to Carl and Bob Weggel — twin brothers who between them carry more than a century of building the magnets that make fusion possible, both veterans of MIT's Francis Bitter Magnet Laboratory, where the Alcator tokamaks were born. Carl designed the Alcator series; one of those machines still holds a Guinness world record for the strongest steady-state magnetic field ever produced. I knew neither of them. I sent the work anyway.

They answered in character, and the division has held ever since: Carl replied on the design, Bob on the mathematics. Bob is the quieter twin — he can sit through a whole meeting and say almost nothing — but he reads everything and proves everything, and every equation in this book passed under his eye before it reached the reader. The field-coil design he handed Kronos is good enough that Brookhaven National Laboratory, where he spent years building record-setting magnets, still asks regularly to collaborate with us.

Carl is our chief scientist, and he became my teacher in fusion. Most of what I know of this field that did not come from a textbook, I owe to him — the physics as it is actually practiced by someone who has spent fifty years building magnets that either hold their field or fail with nothing in between. He taught with a rigor that never condescended: he expected me to follow the argument all the way down, and gave me the room to get there on my own.

The shape of the whole thing

If Carl taught me the physics and Bob proved the mathematics, Dr. Gerald Kulcinski gave the program its shape. He has been with Kronos almost from the start, and he is one of the great figures in the history of this field — to my mind one of the finest scientific minds of his generation. He ran the Fusion Technology Institute at the University of Wisconsin–Madison for decades; he is a member of the National Academy of Engineering; and in his own laboratory he achieved the first steady-state fusion using helium-3 fuel in an inertial-electrostatic device — the low-neutron pathway most of the field had quietly written off. For half a century he has argued that the cleanest fusion fuel, helium-3, is waiting for us on the surface of the Moon. That argument is his life's work. In a real sense, it is also ours.

Much of what I understand about how fusion actually came to be, I learned from him directly — not from the papers but from a man who was in the room for a great deal of it. To take the history of this field firsthand, from one of its pioneers, is a privilege I still don't quite have words for.

And it is Kulcinski, more than anyone, who is the reason this book describes two machines instead of one. Left to my own instincts I might have chased a single reactor. He — with Dr. David Hammer of Cornell, one of the deans of pulsed-power fusion, and Dr. Siegfried Glenzer, carrying the ignition campaign's hard-won realism, pressing in the same direction — kept turning the problem until the answer separated cleanly in two: a breeder that makes the fuel, and a burner that turns it into firm, clean power. The neutrons a fusion machine throws off, he taught me, are not only a hazard to be shielded against; they are a product — a way to breed tritium, to make helium-3, to manufacture the isotopes the world runs short of. The architecture at the center of this book — build the fuel first, then the machine that burns it — was his insight before it was ever our design.

The field's memory, and a debt older than the company

Dr. Steven O. Dean carries sixty years of the fusion program in his memory — he ran the Confinement Systems Division at the AEC and the DOE, and co-founded Fusion Power Associates. But he means something more particular to me than his résumé. Decades ago he worked alongside my great-uncle, P.K. Iyengar, helping to stand up India's atomic program — the same great-uncle who first told me, when I was seven, that fusion was fifty years away. That the man who helped my family's generation build one nuclear program is now, at the far end of his career, helping me build this one, is a symmetry I did not plan and will never take for granted.

There is a strand of this work that runs on computation, and it has a patron I still find it faintly unreal to name. Dr. Jack Dongarra joined us at the end of 2025. He has been a hero of mine since childhood — my car's license plates read MATLAB — because the numerical libraries he built, LINPACK and LAPACK, are the bedrock the world's scientific computing quietly runs on. In 2021 he won the Turing Award, computing's highest honor. That the man who wrote the software beneath everyone else's software now helps design the machine at the center of this book is one of the stranger privileges of getting to build it. He is one of many — the plasma theorists, the materials scientists, the magnet engineers, the naval and defense veterans named in The People Behind the Work — who, for reasons I am still grateful for, said yes.

The part that was not easy

I will not pretend the road was smooth. Building anything real means gathering people, and gathering people means that some of them leave, and a few turn on you. There were partings I did not choose and did not want. There was, once, a threat against my safety serious enough that I have had to think carefully about what belongs in a book and what belongs only in a courtroom. I have chosen, here, to keep the names and the details out of these pages — not because they don't matter, but because this is a book about a machine, and some accountings are better kept where they can be answered properly.

I mention it at all only so that no one mistakes this for an easy story. It was not. The physics, in the end, was the tractable part. The harder work was the human one: convincing people who had every reason to be skeptical, holding a company together through the years when it was only a promise, and continuing when continuing was expensive in ways that had nothing to do with money. I am the third link in a chain that has spent three generations near the atom, and if I have learned one thing from the people in this chapter, it is that the work is worth doing patiently, and worth doing right — even, especially, when it is hard.

Charting the Course to Fusion's Bright Future

Every star you have ever seen is a fusion reactor. The sun that warms your face is a controlled thermonuclear furnace ninety-three million miles away, converting four million tons of matter into pure energy every second, and it has been doing so, without a single day off, for four and a half billion years. All of human history — every empire, every harvest, every love letter and cathedral and quiet ordinary morning — has run on light that fell to us from that fire. The whole of our ambition, from the first cooking flame to the machine on which you may be reading this, has been the slow art of borrowing the sun's power secondhand. The story of this book is the end of secondhand. It is about bringing that fire down to Earth and lighting it here, on purpose, in a chamber we built with our own hands.

When I was seven years old, my great-uncle — a man who had helped run a nation's atomic program — sat in my family's living room and told a room full of children that one day we would light our cities with the fire of the sun. He said it was about fifty years away. I believed him the way children believe the important adults in their lives: completely, and without understanding a word of the physics.

I am forty-two now. He was closer to right than the field's tired punchline ever admitted. And the thing I most want you to take from this book is that the remaining distance is no longer a mystery. It is no longer even a hope. It is a schedule.

That is the real difference between this book and the one I first wrote. In 2024 I asked you to share a dream. Today I am handing you a plan — dated, staged, and unflinching about its own hard parts. We know which machine makes the fuel and which machine burns it. We know the fields, the fuels, the gates. We have solved the gain on paper, published it in the open, and dared the world to find the flaw. We have built the intelligence that keeps the fire safe, and we have said plainly where that intelligence is not yet enough. We have named the year construction begins, the year the first tritium flows, the year the fleet turns on. None of it requires a miracle. All of it requires work, capital, and nerve — and work, capital, and nerve are exactly what our species has summoned, again and again, whenever the prize was large enough to be worth becoming a little braver for.

And the prize here is as large as any humanity has ever reached for.

What the three forties actually mean

The spine of this book is three numbers that all begin with forty, and I want to gather them one last time, because each one answers a different question, and only together do they make a promise worth believing.

Q40. Forty dollars a megawatt-hour. Within forty years.

The first forty is physics. Q40 means a fortyfold energy return — a plasma that gives back forty times the power poured in to sustain the burn. Sit with that ratio for a moment, because it is the hinge on which a civilization turns. For two centuries we have lived by digging up ancient sunlight and setting it alight, spending three units of the planet to get four back. A machine that returns forty for one does not improve that bargain; it abolishes it. That is the target the burner is built around, and it is worth being precise about the ladder that leads there. The breeder, Hyperion, is not a Q40 machine and was never meant to be; its scientific gain sits near 3.4 — enough to run a fuel foundry, and nowhere near enough to run a grid. I say so plainly in its own datasheet, because the honest gap between "gain that breeds fuel" and "gain that powers a civilization" is exactly the gap the field has spent decades blurring. Q40 belongs to the burner — the deuterium–helium-3 tandem mirror — and I want to be exact about what "belongs" means, because the burner chapter shows a first-unit plasma gain nearer 3.5 and an engineering gain of 1.318, not 40. Q40 is the destination that machine line is built to climb toward, not the number the first one prints — reached across generations through low neutron losses, direct energy conversion, a demonstrated plug, and a fleet grinding down its learning curve, with magnetic fields at the plug approaching 26.5 tesla, half a million times the Earth's own field, bottled in a few meters of superconductor. The gap between 1.318 today and 40 at the summit is not a crack in the argument; it is the argument — a first machine that merely works, held to a promise and a clock. Not wishful arithmetic. Engineering, with the receipts attached.

The second forty is economics. Forty dollars a megawatt-hour is the price at which firm, clean power stops being a virtue you pay extra for and becomes, simply, the cheapest thing on the table. That is the number that changes the world, because history does not turn on what is noble; it turns on what is cheap. Coal won because it was cheap. Oil won because it was cheap. Whatever undercuts them will win the same way, and win completely. That number is a destination, not a receipt — I keep the ledgers themselves out of this public book on purpose — but the destination is what disciplines every engineering choice we make. It is why the commercial burner is sized at roughly a gigawatt rather than something grander and harder to finance. It is why the fuel story runs through the Moon. A machine that merely works is a science result, a photograph for the textbooks; a machine that undercuts the price of everything else is a hinge in the history of the species. The difference between those two sentences is the second forty.

The third forty is honesty. Within forty years is the horizon, and it is deliberately, almost stubbornly conservative. Our internal planning basis reaches commercial scale around 2050 — inside three decades from the first shovel, not four. I promise you forty and plan for less. If we beat the clock, and I intend to, you will have lost nothing by my caution. If the hard parts prove harder than I hope, the slack is already in the schedule, in plain view, where you can hold it up to the light. A field that has cried "thirty years away" for seventy of them has forfeited the right to a tight, flattering timeline. So I gave the timeline room to be wrong and still be kept. Awe is easy to sell; a deadline you can audit is not. The third forty is the one that turns a vision into a contract.

The schedule, in one breath

Here is the whole arc, stripped to its dates, because a plan you cannot recite is not a plan you can hold me to.

The design is closed and published now, in 2026 — solved on paper, open-access, reproducible by anyone on Earth who cares to try. Construction of the first breeder begins in the second quarter of 2027. First tritium is targeted for around 2030 — the first fuel our species has ever bred expressly to feed a star of its own making. The first test burner — a roughly hundred-megawatt demonstrator whose only job is to prove the physics of the mirror — begins around 2032. The commercial burner fleet, in gigawatt-class units, begins around 2036. And around 2040 the single constraint that governs everything downstream — the supply of helium-3 — lifts, when helium-3 mined from the lunar soil begins to arrive and the fuel stops being scarce. From there the fleet scales toward roughly ninety units by 2050.

Notice what that sequence is not. It is not a single heroic machine that either works or doesn't — not the all-or-nothing gamble that has broken the hearts of three generations of fusion scientists. It is two machines with two jobs, staged so that the near-term one pays for the long-term one. The breeder is a foundry that makes fuel and materials — tritium, helium-3, fast neutrons — and it is a real business the day it runs, with no need to wait on the grid. The burner is the power story, and it comes later, funded by the foundry, gated on fuel. Each step earns the right to the next. That is what a plan looks like when it is built to survive contact with reality rather than to win a press cycle. It is not a moonshot. It is a staircase — and every step is load-bearing.

Honest about the gates

I will not pretend the road is guaranteed. This book's discipline — its signature — is to name its own edges out loud, and there are three, each delivered in full in the chapter that owns it. The near-term business is materials, not electricity: the breeder is net-negative on power by design, a foundry that breeds fuel rather than feeds a wire. The burner's economics lean on cheap helium-3, which means the Moon, meant to arrive around 2040 — and if that supply is late, the fleet is late. And the burner still has one genuine physics problem left to close, the density it must hold at the end plugs, which is exactly why a test burner comes before the fleet and not after. Beneath all three sits the plainest fact of all: no hardware has been built yet. The gain is solved, published, and reproducible from the design basis, but a solved design is not a running reactor; there is no hardware net-gain milestone before first operation around 2030, and "net gain in 2027" — 2027 is when construction begins — was a claim I retired. This is the discipline that makes the wonder trustworthy: I will dazzle you with the destination and never once lie to you about the road.

Gain solved is a statement about the design. Gain built is a date that has not yet arrived.

Where the intelligence helps, and where it doesn't

Part of what changed between this book and the one I first wrote is that the machine now has a mind keeping it safe — and I want to be as exact about its limits as about its wins, because a fire that hot forgives nothing. Star-plasma at the heart of the burner is among the most violently complex systems human beings have ever tried to command, evolving faster than any human reflex could ever answer. So we taught a machine to answer, and the control chapter lays out the full ledger of how well — the surrogate speedups, the quench-warning gain, the disruption predictor, every figure measured, deposited, and checkable. One number can stand for the rest: a control-barrier safety layer caught every one of three thousand injected limit violations — three thousand for three thousand — with zero escapes across a hundred and fifty thousand steps. These are not projections.

And here is the honest miss, printed exactly where you can see it: our physics-informed equilibrium solver reached two-and-a-half percent error against a one percent target. It is not good enough yet, and I am not going to round it up to make the page prettier. I will also tell you plainly what I told you wrongly last time — that quantum computing would deliver a near-term advantage for this work. It will not, not this decade; the honest near-term quantum contributions are in sensing and diagnostics, and the computational gains come from quantum-inspired classical methods and offline calibration, not from a quantum machine sitting on the control loop. In this program, artificial intelligence is the working engine of control today; quantum computing is a longer horizon; and I would rather correct myself in print than let a beautiful old enthusiasm stand where a true sentence belongs.

What forty dollars unlocks

Now let me tell you what the whole edifice is for — because the tesla and the triple products and the milliseconds are not the point. They are the means. The point is what happens to a world when firm, clean power costs forty dollars a megawatt-hour and never runs out.

Begin with water, because water is the case where energy and survival are the same sentence. Two-thirds of this planet's surface is water we cannot drink, and hundreds of millions of people live thirsty beside an ocean. Desalination is no mystery — we have pulled fresh water from the sea for generations. It is simply too expensive, because it is enormously energy-hungry, and expensive energy makes expensive water. Now collapse the price of firm power, and the price of fresh water collapses with it — not as a charity that lasts exactly as long as the politics do, but as arithmetic that holds on its own, forever. The coastal region that had to ration becomes a region that never thinks about it again. Deserts turn green not by decree but by cost curve. That is what it looks like to loosen the constraint underneath a problem instead of fighting the problem head-on: the problem simply stops being one.

Then follow the same logic outward, because it does not stop at water. The data center that strained a national grid runs instead on power that emits nothing and never flickers — and the machine intelligence of the coming century, the most energy-hungry mind our species has ever built, gets the clean, limitless current it needs to think. The factory, the hospital, the school in the place that never had reliable electricity finally gets it — not as aid, but as the cheapest option on offer. The nations that spent a century, and too much blood, fighting over what came out of the ground wake up one morning and find they no longer have to. When the wellspring of power is the seawater in every harbor and the dust on a neighboring world, the very geography of conflict dissolves. Every one of those is a door, and behind every door is a measure of human freedom that did not exist before we opened it.

And this is only the first room of the house. The same fire that desalinates an ocean and quiets a war is the fire that will one day carry us off this rock for good — because a civilization that has mastered fusion has mastered the only engine compact and potent enough to make the solar system a neighborhood instead of a wall. The reactor that lights a coastal city is the near cousin of the drive that reaches Mars in weeks instead of months, that makes the moons of the outer planets landfall instead of legend. We are, right now, the first generation with a serious blueprint for the fire that lit every star, held in our own hands. What our ancestors could only worship in the sky, we are learning to switch on. That is not hyperbole. That is the physics, followed to where it honestly leads.

That is the part the equations cannot capture and the datasheets cannot hold. A triple product is a number; water for a city that had none, and stars within a human lifetime's reach, are a different kind of thing entirely. The reason to do the unglamorous engineering — the magnet that holds seventeen tesla, the blanket that breeds a surplus, the four hundred meters of mirror, the control loop that never blinks — is that at the far end of all of it is a world with more of the one thing every other good thing depends on. Energy is the input to everything. Make it clean, firm, and cheap, and you have not solved a problem. You have loosened the constraint under every problem at once.

I want to be equally plain about who this is for, and who it is not. This book credits, by name, exactly one outside partner — NVIDIA — because that partnership is genuinely public and the platform under our control system depends on it. Everyone else who has touched this work appears by role, not because their contributions are small but because a public book should name only what is already, cleanly, public, and because the honest thing is to point the reader at verifiable claims rather than at reputations. The stakes here are too large to rest on anyone's authority, my own included. If the argument in this book is right, it is right because the numbers hold when you check them, not because of whose names are attached. And whatever this work earns beyond its costs is directed, by intention, to the care of elephants at The Elephant Sanctuary in Tennessee — a small, deliberate reminder that the whole point of abundance is what you choose to do with it once you have it.

The promise I can actually keep

What I will not do is go quiet, or hedge, or bury the results. Everything in this book has a citation, a dataset, or a deposit behind it, and everything in the versions to come will too. If a number moves, I will tell you it moved. If I was wrong — as I was, in the 2024 version, about how fast quantum computing would arrive — I will print the correction in plain sight, in the same size type as the boast. A field that has cried "thirty years" for seventy of them cannot demand trust. It has to earn it, one verifiable claim at a time. That is the only way I know to build something this important, and it is the one promise I can make today that does not depend on a single gate closing.

My great-uncle did not live to see the machine. My hope — my genuinely held, schedule-backed hope — is that the children in some living room today will not merely hear about fusion the way I once did, as a beautiful rumor half a century off. They will grow up inside its light. They will live in a world with water enough and power enough and a little more peace than the one we have now, they will watch the first ships leave for other worlds on a fire their parents lit, and they will find all of it unremarkable — the way we find the electric grid unremarkable, having never once known the dark.

He gave a room full of children a number: fifty years. I am giving you a smaller one, and a plan to back it, and a standing offer to check my work. That is the whole distance the field has traveled in a single lifetime — from a promise a child took on faith to a schedule an adult can audit.

Energy is freedom. The equations close. The rest is engineering, and the will to finish.

Let's finish it.

The Machines, by the Numbers

Everything in this book eventually comes down to a small set of numbers that either close or they don't. This section is where I lay them out plainly, stripped of narrative, so you can check the argument against the arithmetic. There are three products here, and they are two different machines. The breeder, Hyperion, is a deuterium–tritium spherical tokamak whose job is not to sell electricity but to make fuel — tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons. The burner is a deuterium–helium-3 tandem-mirror generator whose job is to burn that fuel for firm, low-neutron power; it ships in two housings, Aegis for fixed defense installations and MetroVolt for data centers, and the physics under both is the same. Every figure below is public — published open-access and independently reproducible from the design basis. I have deliberately kept money out of these tables. Where economics matter, they show up as an honest gate at the end, not as a number I am asking you to trust.

Hyperion — the Breeder

Hyperion is the near-term product and the cash engine of the whole plan, and it is important to be blunt about what it is: a foundry, not a power plant. On a full engineering balance it is net-negative on electricity — roughly −79 MWe — because the point is the fuel and the neutrons coming out, not the watts. The gain is real and it is modest. A scientific Q of about 3.4 means the plasma returns a few times the power put into it — enough to run a breeding foundry, nowhere near enough to run a grid. That distinction is the honest center of gravity for this machine.

A word on why these particular numbers hang together. The negative triangularity (δ = −0.30) is not a cosmetic choice; it is a way of holding the plasma edge in a regime that stays quieter under load, which matters enormously in a compact, high-field machine. The 8 T on-axis field is delivered by REBCO high-temperature superconducting magnets that see almost 17 T at the conductor itself — the gap between those two numbers is a magnet-engineering story, and it is the hardest thing on the machine. And the TBR of 1.8 is the whole business case in one figure: the blanket makes 1.8 tritons for every one the plasma consumes, so the foundry breeds a genuine surplus. That surplus, about 4 kg of tritium a year, is the product.

Aegis — the Burner for Fixed Defense Sites

Aegis is the burner in its first housing: firm, dispatchable power for fixed installations that cannot tolerate an intermittent supply. It runs the deuterium–helium-3 reaction, which is prized because it is aneutronic in the main channel — the neutron fraction is only about 5.44%, roughly an order of magnitude below a D–T machine. Fewer neutrons means less activation, less shielding, and a longer-lived structure, and it opens the door to direct energy conversion: capturing the charged fusion products as electricity without a steam cycle in the middle. To hold a D–³He plasma you need extreme fields, and Aegis delivers them — nearly 26.5 T at the high-field end plugs.

SpecificationValue
TypeDeuterium–helium-3 (D–³He) tandem mirror
Fusion reactionD + ³He → ⁴He (3.6 MeV) + p (14.7 MeV)
Primary roleFirm, dispatchable power for fixed defense installations
Operating modeDriven (externally heated)
Neutron fraction, f_n≈ 5.44% (low-neutron)

Commercial fleet2036
Build timeFOAK ~3 yr, declining toward ~2 yr at BOAK

The geometry is worth pausing on, because a tandem mirror is a very different animal from a tokamak. It is a long, straight machine — about 440 m end to end — that traps the plasma between two high-field magnetic plugs rather than bending it into a ring. The plugs at 26.49 T do the confining; the central cell at 17 T does the burning. That length is not a flaw to be engineered away; it is what a mirror trades for a simpler, open geometry and a clean shot at direct conversion. The 2032 date is a ~100 MW test unit that exists to prove the physics, and 2036 is when the commercial ~1 GW machines begin. Aegis and MetroVolt are the same reactor in different clothes; the numbers in this table describe both.

MetroVolt — the Burner for Data Centers

MetroVolt is that same burner pointed at a different customer: firm, clean, around-the-clock power for AI data centers, whose appetite for uninterrupted electricity is the defining infrastructure problem of this decade. The core physics is identical to Aegis — same D–³He reaction, same low neutron fraction, same field ladder, same direct conversion. What is different is the deployment story, and specifically how far it can scale, because MetroVolt is where the long-run fleet lives.

Fusion reactionD + ³He → ⁴He (3.6 MeV) + p (14.7 MeV)

The single most important line in that table is the one about fuel. Early burners run on helium-3 made by the breeder, and that supply is limited — enough to prove the machines, not enough to build a fleet. The fleet-scale story, ~90 units and roughly 90 GW by 2050, is gated on helium-3 arriving from the Moon around 2040. Until that supply exists, MetroVolt is a small number of demonstrated machines, not a grid-scale answer. I would rather tell you that plainly than paper over it.

Program Timeline at a Glance

The three tables above describe the machines. This one describes the sequence — the order the dates arrive in, and why each step is allowed to happen only after the one before it has earned it. Read it top to bottom as a single chain: the foundry gets built and makes fuel; the fuel and the revenue pay for a test burner; the test burner proves the mirror; the commercial fleet begins; and the fleet only reaches scale once the fuel constraint lifts. The dates are targets on the honest, deliberately conservative horizon, not promises of a hard early date.

WhenMilestoneWhat it does
2026Design closed and publishedGain solved on paper, open-access and reproducible — no hardware yet
Q2 2027First breeder (Hyperion) construction beginsThe foundry is committed; this is build begins, not net gain
~2030First tritium from the first breederFirst hardware operation (target; 2031 planning basis)
~2032First test burner — ~100 MW demonstratorProves the D–³He tandem-mirror physics before any fleet
by ~2035First few breeders in service (FOAK → NOAK → BOAK)The foundry matures down its learning curve
~2036Commercial burner fleet beginsGigawatt-class units (Aegis, MetroVolt) start being built
~2040Lunar helium-3 arrivesThe fuel constraint lifts and the burner becomes scalable
~2050Fleet at scale~90 burner units (~90 GW); a deliberately small number of breeders

A few things to notice in that column of dates. The first is the gap between 2026 and 2030: the design is solved now, but the first hardware milestone is years away, and nothing in between is a net-gain claim. The second is that the breeder line and the burner line run in parallel, not in series — the foundry is already maturing while the first test burner is being built, because the foundry is what funds the burner. The third is that the single most consequential date is ~2040, lunar helium-3, because everything to the right of it — the whole leap from a few demonstrated machines to a ninety-unit fleet — is gated on that fuel arriving. Slide that date and the far end of the timeline slides with it. Where two dates are shown for the same event (target versus planning basis), the earlier is what we aim at and the later is what we plan around; the honesty of the schedule lives in that pair.

How to Read These

A few conventions, so the tables don't mislead. Q_sci is scientific gain — fusion power out divided by heating power into the plasma — and it is not the same as putting net electricity on a grid; a machine can have a healthy Q and still be a net consumer of power once you account for everything it takes to run. Hyperion is exactly that case, on purpose, which is why its electrical balance is listed as negative and its role as a foundry rather than a power plant. f_n, the neutron fraction, is the share of fusion energy carried by neutrons; lower is better for a power machine because neutrons are the source of activation and structural damage. TBR, the tritium breeding ratio, above 1.0 means the machine breeds more fuel than it burns.

The fusion-reaction rows are the textbook reactions each machine runs, with the energy split between the products shown in MeV — millions of electron-volts, the natural unit for a single nuclear event. Read those numbers as where the energy goes: in the breeder's D–T reaction, most of it (14.1 MeV) rides out on the neutron, which is exactly why the breeder is a foundry and a materials machine; in the burner's D–³He reaction, most of it (14.7 MeV) rides out on a charged proton, which is exactly why the burner can collect it with direct energy conversion instead of boiling water. The whole strategic difference between the two machines is visible in which product carries the energy.

The field numbers come in pairs — an on-axis or central-cell value and a much higher peak value at the conductor — because the magnet always sees a harder field than the plasma does, and the peak number is the one that sets the engineering limit. That is why the tables quote the breeder by its 8 T on-axis value and list the burner's pair explicitly — 17 T in the central cell and 26.49 T at the plug; the smaller number is what the plasma feels, the larger is what the magnet must survive.

The operating-mode rows say driven for every machine: each is externally heated rather than left to sustain itself, which is a deliberate design choice for controllability, not a shortfall. And the build-time rows describe a learning curve, not a fixed duration — first-of-a-kind units take longest, and each later unit is meant to be built faster as the program repeats itself. The dates in the datasheets and in the timeline are targets on a conservative horizon; where a target and a planning basis differ, both are shown rather than the flattering one alone.

Every figure here is a design-basis value from the open-access publications, or a date from the published program plan; none of it is a financial projection, and there are no costs, prices, or margins anywhere in this section by design. The fleet figures describe the shape of the program — a few breeders, many burners, gated on lunar helium-3 — not a return on anything.

The Honest Gates

Numbers in a table can make anything look finished. These three products are not finished, and the discipline of this book is to say exactly where the edges are.

Materials first. The near-term business is fuel and materials, not electricity. Hyperion is net-negative on power and I say so in its own datasheet. It earns its place by breeding tritium and helium-3, and that is a real market — just not the grid.

The burner's economics need cheap lunar helium-3. The physics of Aegis and MetroVolt is solved and published, but the fleet-scale case rests on a fuel that does not yet ship from where it needs to. Terrestrial helium-3 cannot carry a power fleet; lunar helium-3, arriving around 2040, is what makes the burner economic. Take that supply away and the fleet numbers in the MetroVolt table do not stand.

No hardware net-gain before ~2030. The gain is solved, published, and reproducible from the design basis — but no hardware has been built yet. Construction begins in Q2 2027; first tritium is targeted for ~2030. Any claim of a hardware net-gain milestone before then would be dishonest, and this book does not make it. "Gain solved" is a statement about the design. "Gain built" is a date that has not yet arrived.

The Simulation Register & Proofs

A book that asks you to believe in a machine before it is built has one honest option: it must show its work. Not gesture at it, not summarize it, not ask you to trust that the work was done — show it, line by line, in a form a stranger can pick up and check. That is what this appendix is. Elsewhere in the book I make the argument in prose; here I lay out the ledger the prose is drawn from. Every headline number the program stands on has an entry, an origin, and a status, and none of them hides behind me.

I call this the register because that is what it is: a catalog of the individual computational proofs that, taken together, define the two machines. There are dozens of them. Some are a few lines of analysis you could redo on paper. Some are Monte-Carlo scans across tens of thousands of configurations. Some are finite-element stress calculations, some are trained neural networks, some are fault-tolerant quantum resource estimates that took a documented cost model and ran it out to its unhappy conclusion. What they have in common is that each one produces a number, and each number is either right or wrong in a way the open record lets you test. The design is solved in the sense that these proofs close; it is not yet built, and this appendix is scrupulous about the difference.

A word on why this is separate from the machine datasheets and from the sources note. The datasheets tell you what the machines are. The sources note tells you where the open record lives. This register tells you how each number was earned — which proof produced it, by what method, and how far along the road from calculation to hardware it has actually traveled. It is the connective tissue between a claim on one page and the code that generated it on another.

How to read the register

Each entry has four columns. An ID — a short handle (S-series for the shared physics, B for the breeder, L for the burner's tandem-mirror line, R for the REBCO magnets, D for direct energy conversion, A for the AI and control layer) so a claim in the main text can point straight at its proof. A plain statement of what it computes. The headline result, in public numbers only — physics, geometry, scores, never money. And an evidence class, which is the honest part, because it says how much weight the number can actually bear.

Three evidence classes run through the whole register, and the distinction between them is the most important thing on these pages:

  • DERIVED — the result follows analytically, from established physics and a stated reactivity or cost basis. These are the closest to certain, because they do not depend on a simulator being faithful or a machine being built; they depend only on the mathematics being correct, which anyone can check with a pencil and enough patience. A derived result can still be applied wrongly, but it cannot be faked.
  • RECOMPUTED — the number is produced by a deposited, reproducible script. Pull the deposit, run the driver, and the figure regenerates. Some of these reproduce byte-for-byte (the Monte-Carlo engines, the quantum resource estimates, the statevector results, the calibration curves); some, where a trained model is involved, reproduce as a tight tolerance band across fixed random seeds rather than to the last digit, and I say so where it matters. Recomputed means reproducible on paper. It does not mean demonstrated in steel.
  • VALIDATION-PENDING — the number is a design-point target or a physical requirement that no hardware has yet met. These are the frontier. They are not guesses — each is the output of a real calculation — but they name a thing the program must still go and prove against the physical world. The scientific gain of the breeder is here. The burner's end-plug density is here. Honesty demands they be flagged as clearly as the results that are already in hand.

That is the whole scheme. It maps onto the spine of the book: this register is the evidence for Q40 — the fortyfold energy return that is the physics half of the three forties — and it is deliberately conservative about which parts of that case are settled and which are still owed.

Shared and general physics (S-series)

The program opens, in the breeder paper, with a set of results that belong to no single machine. They are statements about any deuterium-burning plasma, and they matter because they clear away a great deal of wishful thinking before a single design choice is made. They are almost all DERIVED, which is exactly why they are load-bearing: they do not ask you to trust a simulator.

IDWhat it computesHeadline resultEvidence
S1Charged-particle self-heating vs bremsstrahlung in a pure deuterium plasmaFour independent routes give 0.984 to 1.121 at 107–109 keV — they straddle unity, so pure D–D sits on a radiation knife-edge and every neglected loss channel is strictly negativeDERIVED
S2Whether plasma gain in a D–D device saturates as confinement improvesBecause photons leave at c, radiation is not a transport channel; gain saturates without bound and the peak fusion-to-bremsstrahlung ratio is only 1.589 at 108 keV (Z_eff = 1)DERIVED
S3The dependence of the radiation ratio on plasma purityThe fusion-to-radiation ratio is affine in Z_eff, not inverse — critical Z_eff = 1.045 at 108 keV — so any impurity-tolerance claim must name the species and the temperatureDERIVED
S4Whether "charged power" and "directed, recoverable power" are the same quantityThey are not; directed power available to direct conversion is strictly less than total charged power, a distinction that governs the entire burner balanceDERIVED

Read S1 and S2 together and you have the reason this program does not chase pure deuterium-deuterium fusion as a power source, however tempting its abundant fuel. The self-heating and the radiation losses are equal to within the uncertainty of the underlying reaction-rate data — the plasma sits on a knife-edge — and even in the best case the fusion power beats the radiation power by a factor of only about 1.6, once, at one temperature. There is no confinement miracle that rescues this, because improving confinement cannot suppress a loss that travels at the speed of light. That is a derived fact, not a modeling opinion, and it is why the question "how much better must confinement get for D–D to work?" is, as the paper puts it bluntly, malformed. S3 does the same demolition to the loose claim that a little impurity does not matter: the penalty is affine, so the tolerance is real but small and must always be quoted with its temperature. S4 is the quiet one that pays off later — the recognition that the charged fusion products carry a birth energy which is not the same as the directed energy you can actually collect at the exhaust, a distinction the direct-energy-conversion work (D-series) turns into its central result.

The breeder — Hyperion (B-series)

Hyperion is a deuterium–tritium spherical tokamak whose purpose is to make fuel, not electricity: tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons for materials qualification. On a full engineering balance it is net-negative on power, and that is by design. The B-series proofs establish that a compact machine can meet a national-scale fuel requirement, and they are candid about the one thing that remains a target rather than a result — the plasma gain itself.

IDWhat it computesHeadline resultEvidence
B1Minimum plasma current meeting a tritium-production duty, scanned across the design spaceAcross 25,200 configurations (checked by an independent aspect-ratio sweep of 2.36 × 10⁶ evaluations), the minimum current for a 1.87–4.0 kg/yr duty falls from 15.52 MA (D–D) to 4.93 MA (D–T) — about a third of a flagship conventional tokamak'sRECOMPUTED
B2The frozen design point (config 22021)R₀ = 1.2 m, A = 2.5, δ = −0.30, I_p = 9.66 MA, B₀ = 8 T, P_fus = 85.04 MW, Q_sci = 3.076VALIDATION-PENDING
B3Tritium breeding ratio vs blanket designBare ⁶Li blanket sub-unity; frozen lever 1.03–1.06 (literal recipe, Be 9.6–11.8 vol%) → 1.18–1.20 (5 cm solid-Be), OpenMC / ENDF-B-VIII.0RECOMPUTED (lever 1.03–1.20) · VALIDATION-PENDING (FOAK measured TBR)
B4Helium-3 yield and the destructive burn-up channelHe-3 is bred independently of the blanket; the destructive n + ³He → p + T channel removes only 0.18 ppm of the helium-3 on the staged-extraction pathRECOMPUTED
B5Equilibrium tritium inventory on site6.2 kg, inside existing civil licensing precedentRECOMPUTED
B6Exhaust handling under negative triangularityNegative triangularity eliminates edge-localized modes (an ELM-free edge is externally demonstrated at δ_avg = −0.5); the trade is a narrow scrape-off layer, λ_q ≈ 0.202 mm and ~14.3 GW/m² upstream parallel heat fluxDERIVED

The heart of the breeder case is B1 and B2, and it is worth being precise about why they carry different evidence classes. B1 is a scan: the program took the governing physics — pressure-limited operation at fixed beta — and asked, across a very large space of machine configurations, what the minimum plasma current is that still meets the fuel-production duty. That the answer for deuterium–tritium (4.93 MA) is a third of the current for pure deuterium–deuterium (15.52 MA) is a recomputed result, because it comes out of a deposited scan you can rerun, and it is cross-checked by a second, independent sweep of over two million evaluations. This is the proof behind the sentence "fuel follows purpose": D–D would make more tritium per unit of fusion energy, but it costs so much more current to run that D–T is the correct breeder fuel anyway.

B2 is different, and I flag it VALIDATION-PENDING deliberately. The frozen design point — configuration 22021, at 9.66 MA, delivering 85.04 MW of fusion power at a scientific gain of 3.076 — closes in the scan. The arithmetic is real and reproducible. But the gain of 3.076 is a design-point target that no device has yet demonstrated: the best any machine has achieved to date is a scientific Q of about 0.7. This is the single most important honesty in the whole book, and I will not let a reproducible calculation borrow the credibility of a hardware result. The gain is solved on paper. It is not built. The register says so in the evidence column, not in a footnote.

B3 carries a split evidence class for the same reason. The lever values are recomputed in the deposited neutronics and is already net-breeding — the blanket makes more tritium than the plasma burns. The headline TBR of 1.8 that the machines are specified to is above that demonstrated figure; it corresponds to an advanced blanket and is carried, openly, as a development target rather than a delivered result. Both numbers appear because hiding the gap between them would be exactly the kind of quiet substitution this appendix exists to prevent.

The burner — the D–³He tandem mirror (L-series)

The burner is the later act: a deuterium–helium-3 tandem-mirror generator that burns the fuel the breeder makes, for firm, low-neutron power, in two housings — Aegis for fixed defense sites and MetroVolt for data centers. Its physics is genuinely harder than the breeder's, and the L-series is where the program is most exposed, because it names an open requirement rather than absorbing it into an optimistic assumption. The 40-year horizon in the three forties, and the $40/MWh that lives with this machine, both depend on the L-series requirements eventually being met — and on cheap lunar helium-3 to fuel it.

IDWhat it computesHeadline resultEvidence
L1Engineering power balance on measured component efficienciesUsing ions-only direct conversion at the best measured ion-tube efficiency (η_ion = 0.470), the device closes with Q_E = 1.318 at the design operating point (x_³He = 0.30), for net +850 to +2832 MWe across the 440–1400 m configurations — provided the end plug reaches the required densityRECOMPUTED
L2Neutron power fraction of the fuel cyclef_n = 5.44% at the design point — low-neutron, roughly an order of magnitude below D–T (not aneutronic); closure holds across x_³He ∈ [0.20, 0.43], with f_n running 9.52% → 2.77%DERIVED
L3The end-plug density the balance requiresPlug-to-central density ratio n_p/n_c ≈ 16 (~4 × 10²¹ m⁻³), roughly two orders of magnitude above any operated tandem-mirror plug — the design's single largest open requirement; at the reference ratio the balance falls to Q_E = 0.63, and pure D–D never closes (Q_E = 0.42)VALIDATION-PENDING
L4Synchrotron reabsorption scalingThe effective harmonic cutoff is not a fixed plasma property but scales as n\* ∝ a^(1/3) — synchrotron loss is a function of machine size, not a fixed fraction of fusion powerDERIVED
L5Why pure deuterium cannot close the balanceThe failure is a charged-power budget, not confinement: charged power is a factor ~5.8 short of the axial loss (697 vs 4055 MW at 440 m, length-independent)RECOMPUTED
L6The end-plug thermal barrierThe one real physics gate: attempted on a historical tandem mirror, which returned a measured negative; it is named as a requirement, not claimed as solvedVALIDATION-PENDING

L1 is the burner's closure proof, and it is honest about being conditional. The balance closes — positive engineering gain, no requirement-class efficiency in the ledger, using only efficiencies that have actually been measured on hardware — but it closes provided the end plug can hold the density ratio in L3. That proviso is the whole game. The plug density needed, n_p/n_c ≈ 16, is about two orders of magnitude beyond anything an operated tandem mirror has achieved, and I mark it VALIDATION-PENDING because it is the largest single open requirement in the program. At the more conservative reference plug ratio the balance does not close (Q_E drops to 0.63). The program does not paper over this; it states the number, states the gap, and calls the thermal barrier that governs the plug (L6) the one real physics gate the burner has to clear.

The genuinely new physics in the L-series is L4, and it is DERIVED because it is a result about how the equations scale rather than a fit to a simulation. The finding is that synchrotron reabsorption — the degree to which the plasma reabsorbs its own emitted radiation — depends on the size of the machine, through the one-third power of the minor radius, rather than being a fixed fraction of the fusion power as the field had generally treated it. That single scaling reorganizes how you think about losses in a large mirror. L5 is the recomputed proof of why the low-neutron advantage of D–³He cannot simply be traded for pure deuterium: the shortfall is in the charged-power budget, and it is a factor of nearly six, which no amount of better confinement closes.

The REBCO magnets (R-series)

Both machines live or die on their high-field superconducting magnets, and the magnet paper's central result is an honest negative — a case where the calculation says this does not close as drawn. That is exactly the kind of result a reproducibility-first program should be proud to publish, and the R-series reports it in full.

IDWhat it computesHeadline resultEvidence
R1Verification of the winding-mechanics methodOne bore-resolved mechanics, validated to 0.8% against a closed-form elasticity solution — an independent ground truth before any design is judgedRECOMPUTED
R2Breeder centrepost magnetStress-comfortable at a realizable ~20 T-on-conductor point (the frozen design’s on-conductor peak for 8 T on-axis); the binding limit here is coil-field and neutron lifetime, not stressRECOMPUTED
R3Burner end-plug magnet — the honest negativeAt its physically required bore (0.648 m), the plug is stress- and strain-bound: peak hoop stress 2.7–3.9× the reinforced allowable and inner-turn strain 4.6–6.5× the 0.40% irreversible cap, with engineered pre-load reducing peak strain by only ~11%RECOMPUTED
R4What the conductor material permits vs what a coil can realizeREBCO's upper critical field exceeds 100 T, so a 35 T operating point is one-third of the material limit — the constraint is winding mechanics and bore, not the superconductorDERIVED

The R-series is a study in keeping two things separate: what the material can do and what a coil can do. R4 is the derived statement that the superconductor itself is nowhere near its ceiling — a 35 T operating field is a third of REBCO's upper critical field. R2 shows the breeder centrepost is comfortable on stress at the field it needs; its real limits are elsewhere (how much field the geometry can produce, and how long the conductor survives the neutron flux). And then R3 is the negative the program refuses to hide: at the bore the burner's high-field end-plug physically requires, the winding is over its stress allowance by up to a factor of four and over its irreversible-strain cap by up to a factor of six-and-a-half, and the usual trick of engineered pre-load buys only about eleven percent of relief. The point of R1 is that you can trust R3, because the mechanics that produced it was first checked against a closed-form solution to within 0.8%. A program willing to publish R3 at full strength is a program you can believe when it publishes a result that closes.

Direct energy conversion (D-series)

Direct energy conversion is the burner's promise of capturing charged fusion products as electricity without a steam cycle. The D-series delivers a genuinely counterintuitive result and is honest that the technique is a bounded upside lever, not the machine's closure mechanism.

IDWhat it computesHeadline resultEvidence
D1The composition of the axial loss stream at reactor temperatureAlthough the 14.66 MeV D–³He proton carries ≈80% of the charged birth energy, at T_i = 80 keV it thermalizes on the electrons before it can escape; the axial exit is a thermalized split — ≈55.5% electron/thermal, ≈44.5% directed ion — an inversion of the received picture that holds across 20–200 keVDERIVED
D2A quasineutral two-species expander to recover the electron channelOne worked embodiment (expansion ratio 20, 5 T → 0.25 T) recovers a bounded ≈28% of the electron channel after realistic demagnetization and detachment losses, without the space-charge back-emission wallRECOMPUTED
D3What the expander actually buys at the plant levelIt lifts axial electric recovery by ≈13% (≈97 MWe) but moves plant energy multiplication only from Q_E = 1.0023 to 1.0026, because Q_E is gated by recirculating plug power, not by DECRECOMPUTED

The D-series is the payoff of S4, the shared-physics observation that directed power is not the same as charged power. D1 is the derived surprise: the fast proton that everyone designs an ion converter around does not, at reactor temperature, arrive at the exhaust as a directed ion — it has already dumped most of its energy onto the electrons, so the loss stream is majority electron, a fact no conventional direct converter is built to recover. D2 proposes and recomputes a device that recovers about a quarter of that electron channel by running an ambipolar magnetic nozzle backward. D3 is the honesty: even done well, this lifts the plant energy multiplication by a few parts in ten thousand, because the thing that actually gates the burner is the recirculating power of the end plug, not the efficiency of the exhaust. DEC is a real lever and a real piece of physics; it is not, and the paper says plainly it is not, the burner's closure mechanism. (These Q_E figures come from the DEC study's own conservative, electron-inclusive balance and should not be read against the burner paper's L1 gain, which uses a different convention — a caution the register makes explicit rather than letting the two numbers collide.)

AI, control, and quantum (A-series)

The control and computation layer is where the program has the most results that are working now, on the digital twin, with hard numbers — and the most disciplined accounting of what does not work. It holds three technology tiers strictly apart: physics-informed machine learning is deployable now, in the loop, when its error is bounded and deterministically clamped; quantum sensing is a near-term diagnostics technology; and quantum computation is, for fusion, an offline calibration tier with no advantage this decade — a point the program makes plainly rather than selling. The program's AI work is developed as a member of NVIDIA's Inception program, the one external partner named in this book.

IDWhat it computesHeadline resultEvidence
